title: Ancient Egypt in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms and roughly when each flourished.
summary: Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years. Its three great kingdoms, Old, Middle and New, were separated by Intermediate Periods when the land split.

cards.headline: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid.
cards.body: That’s how long ancient Egypt lasted. So how do you keep a story that long straight in your head? Start with the big shape.

cards.headline: Peaks and valleys
cards.body: Egypt’s story isn’t one smooth climb. Between the three kingdoms came the First, Second and Third Intermediate Periods, when the country split apart, often into local rule in Upper and Lower Egypt. Each time, the land was eventually pulled back together and a new great age began. Picture a mountain range: historians named the peaks Old, Middle and New. The valleys got the less glamorous name “Intermediate.”
cards.callout: Kingdom, split, kingdom, split, kingdom

cards.context: Count from the first kings, around 3100 to 3000 BCE, to 30 BCE, when Egypt became a province of Rome. That’s one civilization running for longer than the time between Cleopatra and you. Why it lasted so long is this chapter’s story, and it starts with a river.

title: The Gift of the Nile
objective: After this level you can explain why Egypt depended on the Nile's yearly flood.
summary: Summer rains in Ethiopia made the Nile flood Egypt every year, leaving rich silt behind. Herodotus called Egypt “the gift of the river.”

cards.headline: Egypt barely gets any rain. So how did it feed a great civilization?
cards.body: A little over an inch of rain falls on Cairo in a year, and less than that farther south. Yet Egypt fed a dense population and prosperous cities for about 3,000 years. The answer arrived every summer, from somewhere else.

cards.headline: Someone else’s rain
cards.body: Far to the south, heavy summer monsoon rains pour onto the highlands of Ethiopia. They swell the Blue Nile, which does most of the work of bringing the flood downriver. Every year, roughly from July to October, the Nile rose and spread over Egypt’s fields. Egypt’s water supply depended on another country’s rainy season. Imagine your garden being watered by someone else’s storm.

cards.headline: The black gift
cards.body: When the water drained away, it left a layer of dark, fertile silt on the fields: free fertilizer, delivered every year. But the flood had to be just right. Too low, and some fields stayed dry and people could go hungry. Too high, and it could wipe out whole villages. Egyptians didn’t want a big flood or a small one. They wanted a Goldilocks flood.
cards.callout: Too low: hunger. Too high: ruin. Just right: silt.

mascot.line: Herodotus got the quote, the gods got the thanks, and the Ethiopian rain did the actual work.

cards.headline: Whose gift?
cards.body: The famous phrase “the gift of the Nile” comes from Herodotus, a Greek historian who visited Egypt in the 5th century BCE. He actually wrote “the gift of the river,” and he meant the land itself, built up from the Nile’s mud. Egyptians would have thanked someone else: they believed the flood was a gift of the gods. If it came too big or too small, they blamed an angry river or a king who had slipped in his duties.

title: Black Land, Red Land
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between the fertile valley and the desert around it.
summary: Kemet, the black land, was the narrow strip of Nile silt where Egyptians farmed and lived. Deshret, the red desert, held their cemeteries and guarded their borders.

cards.headline: Ancient Egyptians named their country after its dirt.
cards.body: They called it Kemet, “the black land.” All around it lay a second land, Deshret, red and dry. Where one ended and the other began shaped where Egyptians lived, farmed and buried their dead.

mascot.line: Black for life, red for desert. Egypt’s map came color-coded.

cards.headline: The black land
cards.body: Kemet meant the fertile land of the Nile valley, black with the silt the flood left behind (remember Level 2’s gift?). It was a thin green ribbon. Between Cairo and Aswan, the farmland is mostly just 8 to 16 km wide, and in places only a few hundred meters. At the widest of those usual stretches, you could walk from one edge to the other in an afternoon.

cards.headline: The red land
cards.body: Step off the black soil and you were in Deshret, “the red land”: the hot, dry desert. Cities could flourish only where there was water, in the valley, the Delta or a desert oasis. But the red land had its uses. Its dry climate made it an ideal place for cemeteries. Farm on the black, bury in the red.

cards.headline: A wall made of sand
cards.body: The desert had one more job: it guarded Egypt. Deserts lay to the west and east, the Mediterranean to the north, and the First Cataract of the Nile at Aswan to the south. Historians call it a favorable and secure location. Egypt wasn’t cut off, though: it sat at the center of trade routes to western Asia, the Mediterranean and central Africa. It just had very good fences.

title: Farming by the Flood
objective: After this level you can describe the farming year of flood, planting and harvest.
summary: The Egyptian year had three seasons: Akhet (the flood), Peret (plowing and sowing) and Shemu (harvest and low water). Emmer wheat and barley were the main crops.

cards.headline: The Egyptian year had three seasons, and every one was about the Nile.
cards.body: Not spring, summer, autumn and winter. Flood, emergence and low water. Here’s how a farmer’s year ran on the river’s clock.

events.label: The flood covers the fields
The land comes out of the water; farmers plow and sow
Harvest, then a dry spell until the next flood

mascot.line: Best farmhands in Egypt: they worked for grass.

cards.headline: Planting crew: sheep
cards.body: Once the flood drained off, the soil was soaked and freshly fertilized, ready for the plow. Farmers tilled it with a wooden plow pulled by an ox or a donkey. The seed went in from a funnel on the plow, or it was trodden into the soil by sheep. Yes, sheep. Some of Egypt’s planting crew walked on four legs and never asked for wages.

cards.headline: What grew in the mud
cards.body: The main crops were emmer wheat and six-rowed barley, with lentils, beans, onions and flax alongside. Flax mattered more than it looks: Egyptians wove it into linen. When the grain ripened, farmers cut it with sickles, then the river dropped to its lowest before rising again. One flood, one sowing, one harvest. A whole country planted in last summer’s mud.

title: Boats on the Nile
objective: After this level you can explain how the Nile served as Egypt's main road.
summary: The Nile flows north and Egypt’s wind blows from the north, so boats drifted north on the current and sailed south with the wind, as far as the First Cataract.

cards.headline: On the Nile, going south meant hoisting a sail. Going north, you didn’t bother.
cards.body: The river gave Egypt one more gift: a two-way road. The trick was that the water and the wind moved in opposite directions.

mascot.line: Free power both ways. Egypt’s river came with its own return ticket.

cards.headline: A road with two engines
cards.body: The Nile flows north, through northeastern Africa into the Mediterranean. So a boat heading north simply rode the current. Egypt’s wind usually blew the other way, from the north. Raise a sail, and that same wind pushed you south, upstream, against the current. Heading north, you went with the flow. Heading south, you let the wind do the rowing.
cards.callout: North: ride the current. South: raise the sail.

cards.headline: The rulebook in miniature
cards.body: An official named Meketre was buried at Thebes around 1985 BCE with a wooden model riverboat, now at the Met. On it, twelve oarsmen row downstream, north, and the mast is down, because heading north meant pulling against the north wind. Going south, the Met explains, the boat would have been sailed and the rowers could rest. Four thousand years later, the model still follows the traffic rules.

cards.headline: Egypt’s main road
cards.body: The Nile was the easiest way to travel, and Egypt’s great highway for trade, mining expeditions and building projects. Since cities could flourish only by water, Egypt’s towns lined the road. Boats could run the river all the way south to Aswan and the First Cataract, a stretch of rock-strewn rapids that partly blocked the Nile. That was the end of the line, and Egypt’s southern border.

title: Two Lands
objective: After this level you can explain why Egypt was two lands and how the double crown joined them.
summary: Upper Egypt was the southern valley and Lower Egypt the northern Delta. Each had a crown, white and red, and kings wore both as the double crown.

cards.headline: In ancient Egypt, Upper Egypt is in the south.
cards.body: It isn’t a mistake. Egypt was really two lands, and their names only make sense if you think like the river.

cards.headline: Upstream and downstream
cards.body: Egyptians named their two lands by the Nile. Upper Egypt was upstream: the long, narrow valley in the south. Lower Egypt was downstream: the Delta in the north, where the river fans out into several branches before the sea. In late predynastic times, before there was one king, they were separate political lands. On a modern map, the “upper” half sits at the bottom.

cards.headline: One head, two crowns
cards.body: Each land had its own crown. Upper Egypt’s white crown was tall and cone-shaped. Lower Egypt’s red crown was flat, with a rising back and a spiral curl in front. Kings often wore them combined as the double crown, a symbol of both lands united under one ruler. The royal title said it too: “King of Upper and Lower Egypt.” Two lands, one king, and a hat that told you so.
cards.callout: White crown + red crown = double crown

mascot.line: Somewhere, maybe, the greatest hat in history is still waiting to be found.

cards.fact: No real Egyptian crown has ever been found.
cards.context: We know the white, red and double crowns from works of art: statues, paintings and carvings of kings. But no actual crown has survived, so nobody knows for certain what they were made of. For some of the most famous hats in history, that’s quite a vanishing act.

title: Before the Pharaohs
objective: After this level you can describe Egypt's earliest farming villages.
summary: Farming villages appeared in Egypt by about 5000 BCE. Badarian potters followed, villages grew into towns, and Upper Egyptian culture spread north.

cards.headline: Long before the first king, Egyptians were painting boats on their pots.
cards.body: Kings, crowns and pyramids came late in the story. First came farmers, villages and some very good pottery.

cards.headline: The first farmers
cards.body: By about 5000 BCE, villages in the Faiyum were keeping sheep, goats and pigs and growing emmer wheat, barley and flax. Farming in Egypt only really took off once domesticated animals arrived from Southwest Asia. So the first Egyptian farmers borrowed their herds from the neighbors, then put them to work beside the water.

mascot.line: Thousands of years of Egyptian potters, and the village farmers may still hold the crown.

cards.headline: The best pots on the Nile
cards.body: Around 4000 BCE, the Badarian people of Upper Egypt farmed, herded and made remarkable pottery: thin-walled, well fired and black on top. Many experts rate it the best ever made in the Nile valley, which is quite a review for village farmers. They also carved ivory combs and spoons and flat stone palettes. Hold on to those palettes: one very famous palette is coming in Level 8.

cards.headline: From villages to towns
cards.body: Over the following centuries, villages grew into towns. The culture of Upper Egypt spread north into Lower Egypt, probably through trade. Boats are among the earliest designs painted on Egyptian pots, which date to about 3500 to 3300 BCE, so the river road was already part of life. By around 3100 to 3000 BCE, the two lands would share not just a way of life but a king.

title: Narmer and the First Kings
objective: After this level you can describe how Narmer is said to have united Egypt around 3100 BCE.
summary: Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE. Tradition credits Menes; the Narmer Palette shows both crowns, but its meaning is debated.

cards.headline: Egypt’s first king? Egyptians said Menes. The evidence says it’s complicated.
cards.body: Somewhere around 3100 to 3000 BCE, Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom. Working out exactly how, and by whom, is one of history’s great detective puzzles.

cards.headline: The legend of Menes
cards.body: Later Egyptians remembered a first king named Menes, who joined Upper and Lower Egypt and founded Memphis, which became the capital. But Menes is legendary. Historians have tried to match him with real early kings, such as Narmer and Aha, without settling it. He may even stand for several kings. Egypt’s founding father might be a whole committee.

cards.headline: The Narmer Palette
cards.body: The best clue is a carved stone palette found at Hierakonpolis in Upper Egypt, made just before the First Dynasty and now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. On one side, King Narmer wears the white crown; on the other, the red crown. Remember the Badarians’ stone palettes from Level 7? This one was ceremonial, and it’s one of the earliest examples of Egyptian relief sculpture.
cards.callout: One king, two crowns, one slab of stone

mascot.line: A picture can tell the truth about power without being a snapshot of one day.

cards.headline: Real battle or royal poster?
cards.body: So does the palette show the day Egypt was united? Scholars disagree. Some read it as a record of Narmer conquering the north. Others see a ritual statement of conquest, not a real event. The wider evidence suggests unity came gradually, through a shared culture and a series of conflicts over several reigns, rather than one single conquest. One king in two crowns makes a great picture. History was slower.

title: Counting Egyptian Time
objective: After this level you can explain dynasties and the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms.
summary: Egyptians counted years by each king’s reign. Manetho sorted the kings into 30 dynasties, which historians group into kingdoms. Early dates are approximate.

cards.headline: No ancient Egyptian ever wrote a date in “BCE.” They counted by kings.
cards.body: So how do we get from “year 5 of the king” to a date on a timeline? With a priest’s old list, a lot of detective work and one small, honest word: “about.”

cards.headline: Counting by kings
cards.body: Egyptians didn’t count years from one fixed starting point. They counted the years of each king’s reign, then started again with the next king. That works fine while you’re living through it. It gets tricky much later, because the few surviving king lists are broken in places, leave out some awkward rulers and sometimes list rival kings who ruled at the same time as if they took turns.

cards.headline: Manetho’s dynasties
cards.body: Around 300 BCE, an Egyptian priest named Manetho wrote a history of Egypt in Greek. He sorted its rulers into 30 dynasties, grouping kings by things like family ties or where their main royal home was. His book is lost, surviving only in quotes by later writers, yet his 30 dynasties are still the basic framework. Historians then group the dynasties into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms and the Intermediate Periods between them.

mascot.line: “About” isn’t a dodge. It’s historians being honest.

cards.fact: Before 664 BCE, Egyptian dates are approximate.
cards.context: From 664 BCE on, Egyptian dates can be tied exactly to our calendar. Before that, experts’ dates can differ by decades or more. That’s why this chapter keeps saying “about,” and why Level 8 dated unification to around 3100 to 3000 BCE instead of picking a single year.

title: What a Pharaoh Was
objective: After this level you can explain the pharaoh's role as king and as a god on earth.
summary: Pharaoh first meant the palace, per-aa, and named the king only from the New Kingdom. The king judged, kept the gods content and set order in place of disorder; his divinity came with the office.

cards.headline: For most of Egyptian history, nobody called the king “pharaoh.”
cards.body: The word first meant a building. The man who lived in it had a job description no modern ruler would sign up for.

cards.headline: A house, not a man
cards.body: “Pharaoh” comes from the Egyptian per-aa, “great house”: the royal palace. Only in the New Kingdom, from the 18th Dynasty, did Egyptians start using it for the king himself, the way a news report might say “the palace announced.” Before that, he was simply the king, and his official title was the one you met in Level 6: “King of Upper and Lower Egypt.”
cards.callout: Pharaoh: first the palace, then the king

cards.headline: The job description
cards.body: One Egyptian text sums up the king’s role in a single breath: he “is on earth for ever and ever, judging mankind and propitiating the gods, and setting order in place of disorder.” Judge of his people, keeper of the gods’ goodwill, and the one person standing between Egypt and chaos. Try fitting that on a business card.

mascot.line: “A god, sort of” sounds like a dodge. For Egyptians it was a precise answer.

cards.headline: A god, sort of
cards.body: So was the king a god? Egyptians said yes, carefully. His divinity came with the office and was renewed through rituals, but it ranked far below the great gods. The living king was identified with Horus, the falcon god; at death he became Osiris, god of the underworld. To his people he showed the gods on earth, and to the gods he stood for his people: a go-between wearing a crown.

title: Crook and Flail
objective: After this level you can explain the symbols of royal power.
summary: The crook began as a herdsman’s staff; the flail’s meaning is unclear. With the nemes, the uraeus cobra, the royal beard and the crowns, regalia made the office visible.

cards.headline: Egypt’s kings carried a herdsman’s staff. The other prop is still a mystery.
cards.body: Egypt’s kings held a crook and a flail. One has a clear meaning. The other is still an argument.

cards.headline: The king as herdsman
cards.body: The crook began as a herdsman’s staff, a long stick curved at one end. It became a sign of kingship through a simple picture: the king as the herdsman of his people. So Egypt’s ruler was, officially, a shepherd. His flock just happened to be a whole country.
cards.callout: Crook: the king as herdsman of his people

mascot.line: Carried by king after king, and its meaning still slipped away. Egypt keeps a few secrets.

cards.headline: The mystery flail
cards.body: Remember the Narmer Palette from Level 8? The flail already appears on it, and it kept roughly that shape for the rest of Egyptian history. Yet nobody knows for sure what it meant. It has been read as a herdsman’s whip, a symbol of birth, or a tool for gathering a sticky resin called labdanum. The god Osiris holds both: crook in one hand, flail in the other.

cards.headline: Dressed as the office
cards.body: The props came with an outfit. Royal regalia included crowns, headcloths, the royal beard, even an animal tail. The nemes was a folded headcloth whose two lappets fell onto the chest. On the forehead reared the uraeus, a cobra that was the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt. Add Level 6’s white or red crown, and nobody could mistake who was king.

title: Viziers and Scribes
objective: After this level you can explain how officials ran Egypt for the pharaoh.
summary: The vizier, chief administrator and judge, ran Egypt for the king; the New Kingdom had one for each land. Provinces had their own officials, and government ran on writing few could read.

cards.headline: The king was a god on earth. Someone still had to do the paperwork.
cards.body: Treasuries to check, granaries to count, temples to manage, cases to judge. One king couldn’t do it all. So who actually ran Egypt day to day?

cards.headline: The vizier
cards.body: Just below the king stood the vizier, the chief administrator and judge, who reported to the king. As the king’s deputy he oversaw the treasuries and granaries, supervised officials, managed temple affairs and administered justice. Picture a prime minister, chief justice and head of the treasury rolled into one very busy person.
cards.callout: Vizier: the king’s deputy, administrator and judge

cards.headline: Two lands, two viziers
cards.body: At first one vizier served all of Egypt. By the New Kingdom, the Two Lands each had their own: one for Upper Egypt, the southern valley, based at Thebes, and one for Lower Egypt based at Memphis. We know the job in detail thanks to Rekhmire, a vizier under Thutmose III, whose tomb at Thebes spells out his duties. Not every official gets his job description written up for eternity.

mascot.line: Reading was a superpower here. Quietly, you’re using one right now.

cards.headline: Power in a pen
cards.body: Below the viziers, Egypt was divided into provinces called nomes, each with its own officials. And the whole system ran on writing, in a country where about 99 percent of people couldn’t read. No wonder texts urging the young to become scribes promised that the scribe gives the orders while everyone else does the work.

title: Taxes Paid in Grain
objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt collected taxes without coins.
summary: Egypt taxed in grain, cattle, cloth and labor, stored grain in state granaries, set taxes by the flood height, and used no coins until the mid-first millennium BCE.

cards.headline: Egypt ran on taxes long before it had a single coin.
cards.body: So what did you hand the tax collector? Look in your granary. A share of the harvest, a cow, some cloth, or your own sweat.

cards.headline: Taxes you could eat
cards.body: Egypt’s economy ran without money. The state collected produce, stored it and handed it out again. Officials took dues in grain, textiles, cattle and labor, and a share of each field’s harvest went to state granaries, which held massive reserves. Remember Level 4’s emmer wheat and barley? That was the tax. Coins arrived only in the mid-first millennium BCE, brought by foreign powers.
cards.callout: No coins: taxes in grain, cattle, cloth and labor

cards.headline: Taxing the flood
cards.body: How much should a farmer owe? Egyptians checked the river. Nilometers measured how high the flood rose, and a level promising a strong harvest meant higher taxes. It made sense: as Level 2 showed, a low flood could bring hunger, and a very high one could wipe out villages. Egypt was, in effect, taxing the harvest before it had grown.

cards.headline: The king comes to count
cards.body: In the Old Kingdom, the king himself toured the country every year or two, a trip called the “Following of Horus.” (Remember Level 11: the living king was Horus.) He checked each province’s wealth and collected taxes. And if you had no grain to spare, you might pay with your back: ordinary Egyptians could be called up to farm, quarry, and build temples and tombs.

title: Egypt's Army
objective: After this level you can describe Egypt's soldiers, archers and chariots.
summary: Early Egypt fought with local militias; the horse, chariot and composite bow arrived in the Second Intermediate Period; New Kingdom chariots carried a driver and an archer.

cards.headline: For over a thousand years after unification, Egypt fought without chariots.
cards.body: Then came the horse, the chariot and a better bow, and in the New Kingdom Egypt became an empire. How did its army change?

cards.headline: Local militias
cards.body: In early Egypt, soldiering wasn’t a separate career. Civil and military roles blurred, and forces were local militias under their own officials, often including foreigners. In the Middle Kingdom, King Senusret III completed a chain of fortresses at the Nile’s Second Cataract in Nubia, well south of the First Cataract border you met in Level 5.

cards.headline: The horse arrives
cards.body: During the Second Intermediate Period, Egyptian warfare was transformed: composite bows, new daggers and curved scimitars, and above all the horse and chariot. Historians say these brought Egypt, which had been technologically behind, up to the level of southwest Asia. Egypt was late to the chariot. It didn’t stay late.
cards.callout: Second Intermediate Period: horse, chariot, composite bow

cards.headline: Two men and a bow
cards.body: An Egyptian war chariot normally carried two men: a driver and an archer. Chariot bodies were so light that a man could carry one on his shoulder. By the New Kingdom, the army was split into infantry and chariot forces, and it recruited Egyptians and foreign troops alike. The result: a fast, light platform for a bowman.

title: Ma'at: Order and Justice
objective: After this level you can explain ma'at and why keeping order mattered so much.
summary: Ma’at meant truth, justice and cosmic order, against isfet, chaos. Keeping it was the king’s central duty, and the Tale of the Eloquent Peasant shows justice was owed even to a peasant.

cards.headline: In one Egyptian tale, a king keeps a robbed man pleading for justice on purpose.
cards.body: He wanted more of the man’s speeches written down. It’s a story, not a court record, but it’s built around the idea Egypt ran on: ma’at.

cards.headline: One word for everything right
cards.body: Ma’at was truth, justice and cosmic order in one word, and also a goddess, shown as a woman with an ostrich feather on her head. Its opposite was isfet: disorder and chaos. Imagine a single word meaning both “honest” and “the universe working properly.” That was ma’at.
cards.callout: Ma’at: truth, justice, order. Isfet: chaos

cards.headline: The king’s real job
cards.body: Remember Level 11’s job description, “setting order in place of disorder”? That order was ma’at. It was set up at creation and reaffirmed each time a new king took the throne, and the king’s duty was to keep isfet at bay, as the sun god Re did. New Kingdom temple reliefs show the king presenting a figure of Ma’at to the gods: order itself, offered as a gift.

cards.headline: The Eloquent Peasant
cards.body: In a Middle Kingdom tale, a peasant named Khunanup is robbed of his donkeys and goods by Nemtinakht and appeals to the high steward Rensi. The king, hearing how well he speaks, orders Rensi to keep him talking without an answer, so the speeches can be written down, and to feed him and his family in secret. Nine appeals later, the robber’s property is handed to the peasant.

mascot.line: Nine speeches to get your donkeys back. Persistence might be a kind of ma’at too.

cards.fact: “Doing Truth is the breath of life.”
cards.context: That’s the peasant in R. B. Parkinson’s translation, and the Truth he means is ma’at, a word that rings through the whole tale. His point: justice isn’t a favor officials hand out. It’s as necessary as breathing.

title: Royal Women
objective: After this level you can describe the power of royal women and queens.
summary: Queenly roles were shared: the Great King’s Wife, other wives including foreign princesses, and the king’s mother. Tiye rose without royal blood; Sobekneferu ruled as monarch.

cards.headline: Egypt had queens. It just didn’t have one single job called “queen.”
cards.body: The role was shared by several royal women at once, and much about them is unknown, because Egyptian records mostly look at the king. Still, some royal women stepped right into the light.

cards.headline: The Great King’s Wife
cards.body: The most important was the Great King’s Wife: the king’s chief wife and usually the mother of the next king. She ranked just after the king and was often shown beside him, usually smaller. Kings had other wives too, including, from at least the New Kingdom, daughters of foreign rulers sent as diplomacy, and the wives usually lived in the royal harem. The king’s mother could matter as well.
cards.callout: Great King’s Wife: next to the king, and often mother of the next one

cards.headline: Tiye, no royal blood required
cards.body: Tiye wasn’t born royal: her father, Yuya, commanded the chariotry. Yet she became Amenhotep III’s favored wife, and he gave her prominence in state affairs. Her name even appeared beside his on official documents, and scarabs celebrating their marriage still survive. For a queen, that’s the ancient version of being on the letterhead.

mascot.line: Keep her in mind. The next level’s ruler knew exactly who came before her.

cards.headline: A woman as king
cards.body: A few royal women went further. Sobekneferu, at the end of the Middle Kingdom’s 12th Dynasty, is the first woman known for certain to have ruled Egypt as monarch. Not the king’s wife: the king. She wouldn’t be the last, as the next level shows.

title: Hatshepsut
objective: After this level you can explain how Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh.
summary: Hatshepsut went from great royal wife to regent for Thutmose III to crowned king, ruling about 1473 to 1458 BCE in a king’s regalia. Her statues were later broken, for reasons still debated.

cards.headline: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as king and never said why.
cards.body: She never explained why she took the throne. Her temple makes her case instead: it claims her father named her heir, and that the god Amun chose her mother to bear the new ruler.

cards.headline: From regent to king
cards.body: Hatshepsut was the elder daughter of King Thutmose I and married her half brother, Thutmose II, as his great royal wife. When he died, about 1479 BCE, the throne passed to his young son, Thutmose III, and Hatshepsut ruled for him as regent. By the end of his seventh year she had been crowned king herself, with the full royal titles, “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” included. Level 17’s Sobekneferu had done it before her.

cards.headline: Dressed for the office
cards.body: Her early images show a typical queen. Then, after a brief experiment mixing a female body with a king’s regalia, her official portraits switched to a male body with the kilt, crown or headcloth, and false beard. Remember Level 12: the royal beard was part of the regalia. The outfit belonged to the office, and now she held it.

cards.fact: Hatshepsut ruled as king from about 1473 to about 1458 BCE.
cards.context: Her greatest monument was her temple at Deir el-Bahri, built as her funerary monument and dedicated to Amun-Re, where scenes make her claim to the throne. And like every Egyptian date before 664 BCE (Level 9), her reign dates are approximate.

mascot.line: Same broken statues, three different stories. That’s history being honest about what it doesn’t know.

cards.headline: The erased king
cards.body: Late in Thutmose III’s reign, years after her death, her statues were broken and her name was dropped from the official list of kings. Why is debated. Early scholars saw revenge. Later Egyptologists argued he wanted a clean male line, Thutmose I to II to III. A 2025 study says the statues were ritually “deactivated,” as other kings’ were. The pieces turned up at Deir el-Bahri in the 1920s.

title: The Royal Court
objective: After this level you can describe life in the pharaoh's palace.
summary: Palaces were mud brick while temples and tombs were stone, so few survive; Malqata shows how richly painted they were. The royal harem could breed deadly plots, as Ramesses III found.

cards.headline: “Pharaoh” first meant the palace. Hardly any palaces survive.
cards.body: Egypt’s temples and tombs still stand, built of stone. The great house where the king actually lived was mud brick. So what was it like inside?

cards.headline: Stone for gods, mud for kings
cards.body: From the Old Kingdom on, Egyptians built tombs and temples in stone: the eternal houses of the dead and of the gods. Homes were mud brick, and so were royal palaces. The king, god on earth or not, lived in the same material as his subjects. Eternity got stone. Everyday life, even a king’s, got mud brick.
cards.callout: Temples and tombs: stone. Palaces: mud brick

cards.headline: A painted palace
cards.body: The best-preserved royal palace is Amenhotep III’s complex at Malqata, in western Thebes. Its walls, floors and even ceilings were decorated with paintings. So picture plain mud-brick walls holding rooms full of color, right down to the floor under the king’s feet.

mascot.line: A palace plot, solved by a hospital scanner. Some cold cases are very cold.

cards.headline: A household of rivals
cards.body: The court also held the royal harem, where the king’s wives usually lived. That could turn dangerous. One of Ramesses III’s secondary wives plotted to kill him and put her own son on the throne. The conspirators were put on trial, but did the king survive? In 2012, a CT scan of his mummy found a deep knife wound in the throat. The plotters, it seems, got their king.

title: Before the Pyramids
objective: After this level you can explain the flat-topped mastaba tombs that came before pyramids.
summary: Before pyramids, Egyptians built mastabas: bench-shaped tombs with a shaft down to a sealed burial chamber and a chapel above where families brought offerings.

cards.headline: You can walk into an ancient Egyptian tomb in New York City.
cards.body: It stands inside the Met, and it isn’t a pyramid. It’s the older, humbler kind of Egyptian tomb, the one that came first: a mastaba.

cards.headline: A bench in the desert
cards.body: Mastaba is Arabic for “bench,” and from the outside that’s just what these tombs look like: a rectangular block with a flat roof and sloping walls, built of mud brick and, later, stone. Egyptians built them from the very start of the dynasties. Remember Level 3? The dry desert made an ideal cemetery, so that’s where the benches went. But the bench is only the lid.

cards.headline: Upstairs, downstairs
cards.body: A deep shaft ran down to the burial chamber, and after the funeral nobody could reach it. Above ground was a chapel with an offering table and a false door: a carved door that doesn’t open, through which the dead person’s spirit could leave the burial chamber and come back. Relatives and priests came to the chapel to pray and bring food. Upstairs took visitors. Downstairs did not.
cards.callout: Upstairs for the living, downstairs for the dead

mascot.line: Perneb planned for his family to visit. He probably didn’t picture them arriving by subway.

cards.fact: Perneb’s mastaba chapel was bought from Egypt in 1913 and rebuilt inside the Met.
cards.context: Perneb was a palace administrator who built his tomb at Saqqara late in the 5th dynasty. In the Old Kingdom, mastabas were mainly for people who weren’t kings, officials like him. His chapel is the one you can walk into, just as his family once did. Now imagine stacking a few of these benches.

title: Djoser's Step Pyramid
objective: After this level you can explain how Imhotep designed the first pyramid.
summary: Imhotep turned King Djoser’s mastaba at Saqqara into six stone steps: Egypt’s first pyramid and the oldest known monumental stone building.

cards.headline: What do you get when you stack benches, each smaller than the last?
cards.body: Egypt’s first pyramid. It was built for a king named Djoser, and, unusually for something this old, we know the name of the man who designed it.

cards.headline: Stacking the bench
cards.body: Djoser, a king of the 3rd dynasty, began his tomb at Saqqara as a flat-topped mastaba, like the ones in Level 21. Then the plan changed completely. The tomb grew into six steps of stone, each smaller than the one below, rising about 60 m. Picture a wedding cake made by a stonemason. It was the first Egyptian pyramid.

cards.headline: All in stone
cards.body: Until then, Egyptian builders had mixed mud brick with some stone. Djoser’s pyramid was built entirely of stone, and it is the oldest known monumental stone building anywhere in the world. When it comes to big buildings in stone, this is where the known record starts.
cards.callout: The world’s oldest known monumental stone building

mascot.line: He designed the most famous tomb of his age, and his own is still hiding. Archaeologists love a mystery like that.

cards.headline: The architect with a name
cards.body: How do we know who designed it? A statue base of Djoser, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, carries the name and titles of Imhotep, his vizier. Imhotep is often called the world’s first named architect. Later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine, and the Greeks matched him with their healing god, Asclepius. One thing is still missing: his tomb has never been found.

title: The Bent Pyramid
objective: After this level you can explain what builders learned from Sneferu's pyramids.
summary: Sneferu’s builders turned steps into smooth sides. The Bent Pyramid changed angle when cracks appeared, and the Red Pyramid got the angle right.

cards.headline: One of Egypt’s great pyramids changes its angle halfway up.
cards.body: It’s called the Bent Pyramid, and it isn’t a ruin or a joke. It’s a record, in stone, of builders learning how to make a pyramid with smooth sides.

cards.headline: Filling in the steps
cards.body: Djoser’s pyramid had steps. Sneferu, the first king of the 4th dynasty, wanted a true pyramid, with smooth, sloping sides. At Meidum, a step pyramid was reworked into a true one. Then at Dahshur his builders started the first pyramid designed as a true pyramid from the very beginning. That’s where things got bent.

mascot.line: Changing the plan halfway isn’t failure. It’s engineering with the lights on.

cards.headline: A change of plan
cards.body: The Bent Pyramid starts steep, at 54 degrees. But as it rose, cracks and structural faults appeared, and about halfway up the builders cut the angle to 43 degrees. The top half is noticeably flatter than the bottom. It looks as if someone got nervous in the middle, and someone did. Their nerves are still visible today.
cards.callout: 54 degrees below, 43 degrees above

cards.headline: Third time right
cards.body: Sneferu’s builders tried again just to the north. The Red Pyramid rises at 43 degrees, the Bent Pyramid’s safer top angle, all the way up. It is the earliest tomb known to have been designed and built as a true pyramid throughout. That made three major pyramids for one king. His son Khufu inherited the lessons, and took them to Giza.

title: The Great Pyramid
objective: After this level you can describe the Great Pyramid of Giza and its size.
summary: Khufu’s Great Pyramid was about 146 m tall, built of some 2.3 million blocks, and the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.

cards.headline: For about 3,800 years, nothing people built stood taller.
cards.body: Not a temple, not a tower, not a city wall, anywhere on Earth. So what exactly did Sneferu’s son put up at Giza?

cards.fact: The Great Pyramid was originally about 146 m tall.
cards.context: It was built for Khufu, second king of the 4th dynasty, and finished in the early 25th century BCE. For an estimated 3,800 years it was the tallest structure humans had made. It is a little shorter today, and the reason is on its surface.

cards.headline: A mountain of blocks
cards.body: About 2.3 million blocks of stone were cut, moved and fitted together to build it. Each side of the base runs about 230 m. Stroll once around the bottom and you’ve walked about 920 m, nearly a kilometer, without going up a single step.
cards.callout: About 2.3 million blocks

mascot.line: Six wonders gone. The pyramids are still here, looking unbothered.

cards.headline: It used to shine
cards.body: The rough, stepped surface in today’s photos isn’t what Egyptians saw. Polished limestone casing stones once made the sides smooth and gleaming. Most of that casing was later removed, and together with erosion, that’s why the pyramid is shorter now. It has outlasted the whole list it belongs to: of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, the pyramids of Giza are the only one still standing.

title: Who Built the Pyramids?
objective: After this level you can explain the evidence that paid workers, not slaves, built the pyramids.
summary: The builders’ own tombs, their healed bones and Merer’s logbook show the pyramids were built by Egyptian workers, called up in rotating crews and paid, not by slaves.

cards.headline: Slaves under the whip? Archaeologists went looking. They found graves.
cards.body: In 1990, a tourist’s horse stumbled on a mud-brick wall near the Giza pyramids. Behind it lay the cemetery of the people who built them.

cards.headline: Tombs beside the king
cards.body: The cemetery holds hundreds of small graves of laborers, plus bigger tombs for overseers and craftsmen, with job titles like “overseer of the side of the pyramid.” Zahi Hawass, who excavated them, put the point simply: “If they were slaves, they would not have been able to build their tombs beside their king’s.” Slaves don’t get a spot next to the king.

cards.headline: What the bones say
cards.body: Their skeletons show backs and knees worn down by heavy work. They also show broken arms and legs that healed after being splinted, so someone was treating their injuries. The builders were Egyptians, many of them called up to serve rotating terms of work for the king under skilled craftsmen, and they were paid for it. Think national service, not chain gang.
cards.callout: Hard work, rotating crews, and someone to set a broken arm

mascot.line: The best evidence isn’t a legend about the builders. It’s their own paperwork.

cards.headline: A worker’s logbook
cards.body: In 2013, Pierre Tallet’s team found the oldest known inscribed papyri at Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea coast. Among them was the logbook of Merer, an inspector who led a crew in Khufu’s reign. He reported to the noble Ankhhaf, Khufu’s half-brother, and his crew was supplied with food by the state. It reads less like a slave story and more like a shipping company’s paperwork.

title: Moving the Stones
objective: After this level you can explain the leading ideas for how huge blocks were moved.
summary: Stone came by boat on the Nile, slid on sledges over wetted sand and went up ramps like the one found at Hatnub; exactly how the ramps worked is still debated.

cards.headline: 2.3 million blocks. No cranes, no trucks. So how?
cards.body: Part of the answer is still debated. But three big clues have turned up: a logbook, a painting and a ramp.

cards.headline: First, a boat
cards.body: Remember Merer from Level 25? His logbook records his crew carrying limestone by boat from the quarries at Tura to Giza. Level 5’s river road was essential for building projects, and here it is doing exactly that. Before a block was dragged anywhere, it often floated.

cards.headline: Water on the sand
cards.body: On land, blocks rode on wooden sledges. A wall painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep shows a man on the front of a sledge pouring water onto the sand ahead of it. In 2014, University of Amsterdam physicists tested the idea: damp sand is about twice as stiff as dry sand, so it doesn’t pile up in front. The right amount of water halves the pulling force. Try dragging a sled on dry beach sand, then near the waves.
cards.callout: The right amount of water halves the pull

mascot.line: We know the tools. We’re still arguing about the layout. That’s honest archaeology.

cards.headline: Up the ramp
cards.body: Raising blocks up the pyramid is the most debated part. Archaeologists generally agree ramps were used, but not how they worked. In 2018, researchers reported a steep ramp at the Hatnub alabaster quarry, flanked by two staircases with post holes. Ropes tied to posts helped haul sledges up slopes of 20 percent or more. It dates at least to Khufu’s reign, so the trick was known while the Great Pyramid rose.

title: The Great Sphinx
objective: After this level you can describe the Sphinx and what we know about it.
summary: The Great Sphinx was carved from a block left in a quarry at Giza. Most scholars credit Khafre in the 4th dynasty; much later, Thutmose IV cleared its sand.

cards.headline: The Great Sphinx wasn’t built. It was left behind.
cards.body: Workers cut stone away around a lump of rock, and the lump became a lion with a human head. Here’s what we know about it, and how we know.

cards.headline: Carved, not stacked
cards.body: The Sphinx is about 73 m long and 20 m high, carved from a single mass of limestone. When workers quarried a ditch in the Giza bedrock, they left a large block standing, and that block became the Sphinx: the body of a resting lion with a human head in a royal headdress. After all those hauled blocks, here’s a monument nobody had to move.

cards.headline: Whose face?
cards.body: Most scholars date the Sphinx to the 4th dynasty and credit King Khafre, who built his own pyramid at Giza. The Sphinx was likely part of his funerary complex. Mark Lehner mapped it and the nearby temples stone by stone and concluded that Khafre’s workers began shaping the Sphinx as they built his valley temple. So the face probably shows Khafre himself.

mascot.line: Napoleon gets blamed for a lot. The nose is one thing he didn’t do.

cards.headline: Noses and dreams
cards.body: The nose is missing, but don’t blame Napoleon: drawings made before his troops reached Egypt already show it gone. Much later, Thutmose IV set up a stone slab, the Dream Stela, at the Sphinx. On it he says the god promised to make him king if he cleared away the sand around the Sphinx. Restoration work may have started in his reign. Useful dream, if you want a crown.

title: Pyramid Towns
objective: After this level you can describe the workers' towns near the pyramids.
summary: South of the Sphinx lay the builders’ town: galleries for crews serving their term, bakeries and silos, and meat enough to feed thousands.

cards.headline: Thousands of people built the pyramids. Where did they sleep?
cards.body: And who cooked dinner? In 1988, a team led by Mark Lehner started finding out, just south of the Sphinx.

cards.headline: The Lost City
cards.body: About 400 m south of the Sphinx, Lehner and AERA found a large settlement: the base for building the pyramid complexes of Menkaure, Khafre and probably Khufu. Laborers, craftsmen, managers and administrators all lived there. It sits by a huge stone wall known in Arabic as Heit el-Ghurab, the “Wall of the Crow.” Archaeologists call it the Lost City of the Pyramids. It was a company town, and the company was the king.

cards.headline: Bunks for a crew
cards.body: Long buildings called galleries run through the town. Each may have housed a za, a crew of 40 men, while they served their term of compulsory work for the king. That fits Level 25’s picture: crews rotating in, doing their stint, and going home. Think dormitory, not dungeon.
cards.callout: One gallery, one crew of 40

mascot.line: Pyramids were built on bread and beer. Also on a very serious amount of mutton.

cards.headline: Bread, beer and beef
cards.body: The town ran on food. Its streets were lined with bakeries, kitchens and warehouses, and royal silos held the grain for bread and beer. Animal bones suggest that on average more than 4,000 pounds of cattle, sheep and goat meat was slaughtered every day. The gallery crews ate mostly sheep and goat. Nobody hauls stone on an empty stomach.

title: Why Pyramids Stopped
objective: After this level you can explain why later pharaohs were buried in hidden tombs instead.
summary: A pyramid advertised treasure. Later pyramids were smaller, robbers beat even Amenemhat III’s maze, and New Kingdom rulers chose hidden tombs instead.

cards.headline: A pyramid is the biggest “treasure here” sign ever built.
cards.body: That was the problem. The sheer size of a pyramid made it a target for tomb robbers. So how do you protect a king?

cards.headline: Smaller and softer
cards.body: Kings kept building pyramids for a long time, but later pyramids were smaller and not as well built. In the Middle Kingdom, Amenemhat III built his pyramid at Hawara of mud brick, with only a casing of white limestone. After Khufu’s 2.3 million stone blocks, that’s mud brick wearing a stone coat.

cards.headline: The maze that failed
cards.body: Amenemhat III tried to beat the robbers with a maze of passages around his burial. It didn’t work: robbers found their way through and emptied the sarcophagi. When the archaeologist Flinders Petrie worked out their route, he concluded they must have had the plan from an informer. The best lock fails when someone sells the key.
cards.callout: Robbers got in anyway, probably with inside help

mascot.line: A pyramid says “look at me.” A hidden tomb says nothing at all. Robbers noticed the difference.

cards.headline: Hide it instead
cards.body: So kings changed tactics. Because of the robbers, New Kingdom rulers were buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings, instead of under a mountain of stone. The lesson of the pyramid age: a tomb everyone can see is a tomb everyone can find.

title: Many Gods
objective: After this level you can describe Egypt's main gods and how they were pictured.
summary: Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods, shown as humans, animals or animal-headed humans. The animal said something about the god: falcon Horus, jackal Anubis, ibis Thoth.

cards.headline: A falcon-headed god, a jackal-headed god, a goddess with a cow’s head.
cards.body: At first glance, Egypt’s gods look like a riddle. To Egyptians, every head was a clue. Here’s how to read them.

cards.headline: A very crowded heaven
cards.body: Over Egypt’s long history, people worshipped hundreds of gods and goddesses. Remember Level 2? Egyptians believed even the Nile’s flood was a gift of the gods. Gods could be pictured as humans, as animals, or as a mix: an animal’s head on a human body. They could even be combined. Amun and Ra joined as Amun-Ra, for more than a thousand years Egypt’s principal god. Two gods, one name, no paperwork.

mascot.line: Once you can read the heads, a temple wall starts introducing everyone by name.

cards.headline: Read the head
cards.body: Egyptians saw certain animals as forms of particular gods, and the animal said something about the god’s nature. Horus, a falcon or falcon-headed man, embodied kingship. Anubis, a jackal or jackal-headed man, cared for the dead. Thoth, god of writing and wisdom, was an ibis or ibis-headed man, sometimes a baboon. Hathor, often a cow, was linked with motherhood. The head works like a name badge: spot the beak, know the god.

cards.fact: The ankh was the Egyptian sign for “life.”
cards.context: Look at almost any picture of Egyptian gods and you’ll spot it: a cross topped by a loop. It was the hieroglyph for “life,” and gods and pharaohs are often shown holding it or offering it. Of all the things a god could hand you, that’s the big one.

title: Ra and the Sun
objective: After this level you can explain the sun god Ra's daily journey.
summary: Egyptians believed Ra sailed across the sky by day and through the underworld by night, beating the serpent Apophis to be reborn every dawn.

cards.headline: Every sunset, Egyptians believed, the Sun set off on a dangerous night voyage.
cards.body: And every sunrise meant it had made it back. Meet Ra, the sun god, and the trip he made every single day.

cards.headline: The Sun takes the boat
cards.body: Ra was the god of the Sun and a creator god, worshipped above all at Heliopolis. He was often shown as a man with a falcon’s head and a sun disk on top. Egyptians believed he crossed the sky each day in a boat, his solar bark. That fits a land whose great highway was the Nile, where boats were the easiest way to travel (remember Level 5?). If you lived by the river, why would the Sun walk?

mascot.line: Next time you watch a sunrise, remember: to an Egyptian, the Sun had just survived the night.

cards.headline: The night shift
cards.body: At sunset, Ra didn’t clock off. Egyptians believed he boarded another boat and sailed through the underworld all night. Waiting there was his great enemy, Apophis, an evil serpent. Ra had to defeat the serpent every night to be born again for the new day. So a sunrise wasn’t just morning. It was a victory, won in the dark, every single day.
cards.callout: Day: sail the sky. Night: beat the serpent. Dawn: born again.

cards.fact: Egyptians believed the Sun was born again every morning.

title: Osiris and Isis
objective: After this level you can retell the myth of Osiris and Isis.
summary: Seth killed his brother Osiris; Isis gathered his body, Anubis made the first mummy, Horus avenged his father, and Osiris became ruler of the dead.

cards.headline: Egypt’s greatest myth begins with a murder in the royal family.
cards.body: A king, a jealous brother, a wife who won’t give up and a son out for justice. It’s the story Egyptians told about death, and about getting past it.

cards.headline: A jealous brother
cards.body: In the myth, Osiris ruled Egypt as king. His brother Seth was lord of the desert and a master of storms and disorder: Deshret, the red land from Level 3, with a face. Jealous Seth tricked Osiris into a chest and threw it into the river. Later he cut the body into 14 pieces and scattered them across Egypt. Chaos had beaten order. For now.

cards.headline: Putting a god back together
cards.body: Isis, Osiris’s wife, would not give up. With her sister Nephthys, she sought out and gathered the pieces. Anubis, the jackal-headed god, embalmed and wrapped the body, making the first mummy. Isis conceived a son, Horus. And Osiris lived on, not in this world but in the underworld, as its ruler and judge. In this story, death is more like a change of address.

mascot.line: A story about one god became a plan for everyone. That’s a very hardworking myth.

cards.headline: A myth with your name in it
cards.body: Horus grew up, fought Seth, avenged his father and became king. Egyptians mapped the story onto real life: the living king was identified with Horus, the dead king with Osiris. Later, every Egyptian, not just kings, was linked with Osiris at death. The myth turned into a promise: what happened to Osiris could happen to you.

title: Temples
objective: After this level you can explain what happened inside Egyptian temples.
summary: A temple was a god’s house, the god living in a statue in a dark sanctuary. Priests dressed and fed it daily; ordinary people saw it at festivals.

cards.headline: An Egyptian temple wasn’t built for crowds. It was built for one resident.
cards.body: Egyptians believed the god actually lived there. And like any honored resident, the god expected to be dressed and served breakfast.

cards.headline: A house for a god
cards.body: A temple was a house for its god, and Egyptians believed the god lived within its statue, kept in a shrine deep inside. Walk in from the gate and the building closed in around you: the sanctuary was the darkest, most enclosed part, with the highest floor. Most people never got close. Non-priests may have been allowed no farther than the open court. The god’s house had a very strict door policy.

cards.headline: Breakfast for a god
cards.body: Every morning the high priest, acting for the king, opened the shrine and greeted the statue with hymns. He dressed it in fine cloth and jewelry and presented it with food. None of it went to waste: the leftover offerings were divided among the priests as part of their wages. The god was served first. The staff ate after.
cards.callout: Open, greet, dress, feed, repeat tomorrow

cards.headline: The god goes out
cards.body: Festivals were different. Priests carried the god’s statue out of the sanctuary in a barque, a portable shrine shaped like a boat. For ordinary Egyptians, this was the chance to glimpse the god. Remember Ra, who crossed the sky by boat in Level 32? On festival days, a temple’s god traveled by boat too, carried by priests.

title: Mummies
objective: After this level you can explain how and why Egyptians mummified the dead.
summary: Egyptians believed the ka and ba needed a preserved body. Over about 70 days, embalmers removed organs, dried the body in natron and wrapped it in linen.

cards.headline: The first Egyptian mummies were made by the desert, not by people.
cards.body: Early bodies buried in shallow pits in the sand were dried out by its heat. Remember Level 3: the red land’s dry climate made it ideal for cemeteries. Later, Egyptians learned to do on purpose what the desert did by accident.

cards.headline: Why keep a body?
cards.body: Egyptians believed a person’s soul had several parts. The two most important, the ka and the ba, needed a well-preserved body they could recognize and return to. Without it, they could not survive. And there was a model to follow: in Level 33’s myth, Anubis embalmed and wrapped Osiris, making the first mummy. Every embalmer after that was copying a god.

But the heart was usually left inside, because Egyptians saw it as the center of knowledge and emotions. The wrappings were linen, woven from flax like the flax farmers grew in Level 4. title: The Weighing of the Heart
objective: After this level you can explain how Egyptians believed the dead were judged.
summary: Egyptians believed the heart was weighed against the feather of Maat. Ammit ate a heart that failed; those who passed reached the Field of Reeds.

cards.headline: After death, Egyptians believed, your heart went on the scales.
cards.body: On the other side of the balance sat a single feather. What happened next decided your forever.

cards.headline: The scene
cards.body: Picture a Book of the Dead made for Hunefer, a royal scribe, around 1275 BCE, now in the British Museum. Anubis brings Hunefer in and supervises the scales. On one side sits his heart. On the other, the feather of Maat, which stood for truth and right order. Ibis-headed Thoth records the verdict. Remember why embalmers left the heart inside the body in Level 35? Here is where it gets its big moment.

mascot.line: Three of Egypt’s most dangerous animals in one body. You really wanted that feather to win.

cards.headline: The Devourer
cards.body: Crouched by the scales waits Ammit, the Devourer: a crocodile’s front, a lion’s middle and a hippopotamus’s rear. If the heart failed, Ammit ate it, and the afterlife was lost. At the judgment, the dead also declared to each of 42 judges that they had not committed a particular wrong, a text now called the Negative Confession. Picture a job interview where you list everything you didn’t do.

cards.headline: Paradise looks familiar
cards.body: Pass, and Horus presents you to Osiris, judge of the dead. Beyond lay the Field of Reeds, imagined as a perfect version of Egypt, with clear rivers, bright sun and plentiful crops to harvest. So even in paradise there was a harvest to bring in, just as Level 4’s farmers cut their crops with sickles. Egyptians pictured paradise as home, only better.

cards.body: It was a roll of spells: a guidebook and protection kit for the hardest journey an Egyptian expected to make.

cards.headline: Spells for the road

Some kept you from losing your head or your heart. Others protected you from snakes, crocodiles and insects along the way. Spell 125 covered the judgment before Osiris from Level 36. cards.body: Scribes copied the spells onto rolls of papyrus, often colorfully illustrated, and sold them for burials. No papyrus contains every spell. You could buy a ready-made copy with blank spaces for your name, or pay more and probably choose your own spells. On papyrus, the spells reached far more people than ever before, though a fine illustrated copy was expensive. Afterlife insurance came in standard and deluxe.

title: Animal Mummies
objective: After this level you can explain why Egyptians mummified cats, ibises and crocodiles.
summary: Egyptians mummified pets, food, sacred animals and, by the million, offerings to gods: almost 8 million animals in the Catacombs of Anubis alone.

cards.headline: One set of tunnels at Saqqara held almost 8 million mummified animals.
cards.body: Most of them were dogs. Egyptians didn’t just mummify people. So why would anyone wrap up millions of animals?

cards.headline: Four reasons to wrap an animal
cards.body: Egyptian animal mummies came in four kinds. Pets were buried to keep their owners company. Food went along for the afterlife. Sacred animals were linked with particular gods. And then there were offerings. Pilgrims bought a mummified animal as a gift to a god: a cat for Bastet, an ibis for Thoth, a crocodile for Sobek. Dedicating one seems to have counted as a pious act: a prayer you could hold in your hands.

cards.headline: Tunnels full of prayers
cards.body: Remember Level 31’s jackal-headed Anubis and ibis-headed Thoth? Their animals were buried by the million. The Catacombs of Anubis at North Saqqara held almost 8 million animals, most of them dogs. Thoth’s ibises filled other tombs: about 1.75 million at Saqqara and about 4 million at Tuna el-Gebel. Each little bundle was one person’s gift to a god, and together they filled underground cities.
cards.callout: One bundle, one prayer. Millions of bundles.

mascot.line: X-rays: helping archaeologists unwrap gifts without ruining the wrapping.

cards.headline: Not always what it seems
cards.body: Modern scans hold a surprise. Scanning hundreds of animal mummies, a University of Manchester team found that around a third contained no animal material at all. From the outside, a bundle looked like a bird or a cat. Inside, a third of the time, no animal at all. A good reminder that a mummy’s label isn’t always its contents, and that scans can check without unwrapping.

title: Amulets and the Scarab
objective: After this level you can explain lucky charms like the scarab and the Eye of Horus.
summary: The scarab stood for Khepri, who rolled the Sun like a dung ball: rebirth. Heart scarabs silenced the heart at judgment; the wedjat eye protected.

cards.headline: Egypt’s favorite lucky charm was a dung beetle.
cards.body: Not a lion. Not a falcon. A beetle that rolls balls of dung. To Egyptians, it carried one of the biggest ideas they had.

cards.headline: The beetle that rolls the Sun
cards.body: Watch a scarab push its ball of dung along the ground, and Egyptians saw the god Khepri rolling the Sun across the sky. Khepri, the scarab god, stood for creation, rebirth and the morning sun: the Sun reborn after Ra’s night voyage through the underworld in Level 32. Young beetles even seemed to come out of the dung ball as if self-created. A small insect, a very big idea.

mascot.line: Even your heart got a little pep talk before the big day.

cards.headline: A word with your heart
cards.body: Scarabs were the most numerous Egyptian amulets, and most were made for the living. But one kind went with the dead. A heart scarab, placed with the mummy, carried a Book of the Dead spell telling the heart not to stand up as a witness against its owner. Remember the scales in Level 36? This was insurance against your own heart telling on you.

cards.headline: The eye that healed
cards.body: Another favorite was the wedjat eye. In the myth from Level 33, Seth damaged Horus’s eye in their fight, and it was healed. Wedjat means “the sound one.” It became one of Egypt’s most popular amulets, used for protection by the living and the dead. Amulets like these were often tucked into a mummy’s linen wrappings: small charms for a long trip.

title: Hieroglyphs
objective: After this level you can explain how hieroglyphs mix sound signs and picture signs.
summary: Hieroglyphs look like pictures, but most signs stood for sounds (consonants only), while meaning signs such as determinatives told readers what kind of word they were reading.

cards.headline: In hieroglyphs, a picture of a house could help you write “go out.”
cards.body: It sounds like a riddle, but it’s the key to the whole system. Hieroglyphs look like pictures. Most of the time, they weren’t being used as pictures at all.

cards.headline: Mostly sounds
cards.body: A hieroglyph could show the thing it pictured, but usually a sign stood for a sound: one, two or three consonants. Vowels weren’t written at all, so readers supplied them, the way you can still read “prmd” as pyramid. About 700 signs stayed in use for more than 2,000 years. That’s a lot to learn, but far fewer than a picture for every word would need.
cards.callout: Most signs spell sounds. Some carry meaning. Few are just pictures.

mascot.line: Walking legs for a word about moving. Honestly, very sensible.

cards.headline: Signs that steer the meaning
cards.body: Some signs carried meaning instead of sound. The sun sign could also mean “day,” or name the sun god Re. Others were helpers called determinatives, added to show what kind of word you were reading. The house sign also spelled the sound pr, and it helped write the verb “to go out.” Add a pair of walking legs, and you knew which word was meant: this one is about moving.

cards.headline: Which way do I read?
cards.body: Hieroglyphs usually ran from right to left, but not always. The signs tell you: the way they face shows the reading direction, so the birds and people act as arrows. The system itself appeared in the late predynastic period, just before Egypt’s First Dynasty, as the Two Lands were becoming one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE. Egypt got a king and a script at about the same time.

title: Papyrus
objective: After this level you can explain how papyrus was made from reeds.
summary: Papyrus sheets were made from crossed strips of a Delta marsh plant, pressed so its own sap glued them, then pasted into rolls. The oldest known roll is blank.

cards.headline: The word “paper” comes from a reed that grew along the Nile.
cards.body: Long before paper mills, Egyptians wrote on sheets made from a marsh plant, and the plant supplied its own glue. Here’s how a reed became a notebook.

cards.headline: A reed for everything
cards.body: Papyrus grew thick in marshes, and Egyptians cultivated it in the Nile Delta. It was a do-everything reed: people made rope, mats, sandals and even boats from it. Remember Level 6? The Delta was Lower Egypt, the northern of the Two Lands. So Egypt’s writing material grew in the north, in the same marshes where the river fans out toward the sea.

cards.headline: Strips, cross, press
cards.body: To make a sheet, workers cut the stem’s inner pith into long strips and laid them side by side. A second layer went on top at right angles. The sheet was dampened and pressed, and the plant’s own gluelike sap cemented the layers together. Then it was hammered and dried in the sun. No glue pot needed: the plant glued itself.
cards.callout: Lay, cross, press, hammer, dry

mascot.line: Somewhere, a scribe is still meaning to get round to it.

cards.fact: The oldest known papyrus roll, from about 2900 BCE, is blank.
cards.context: It comes from the First Dynasty tomb of an official named Hemaka. Sheets were pasted into rolls, usually no more than 20 sheets long, ready for writing. This one never got a single word. Egypt’s oldest surviving roll, and nobody wrote in it.

title: Scribes
objective: After this level you can describe how scribes trained and worked.
summary: Scribal schools taught reading, writing and math, above all the cursive hieratic script. Scribes wrote with reed brushes in black and red ink, and their rare skill set them above most Egyptians.

cards.headline: Probably fewer than 1 Egyptian in 100 could read. Scribes could.
cards.body: That made writing a rare skill, and a powerful one. So how did you become one of the few, and what did you carry to work?

cards.headline: Scribe school
cards.body: Young men enrolled in scribal schools to learn the trade: reading, writing and the basics of math. The script they drilled most was hieratic, a flowing, cursive form of the hieroglyphs from Level 41, written on papyrus, broken pottery and flakes of stone. Hieroglyphs were for monuments and display. Hieratic was for getting work done, the way you print neatly on a poster but scribble in a notebook.

mascot.line: Red for mistakes. Some things never change, and maybe they shouldn’t.

cards.headline: The original red pen
cards.body: A scribe’s main tool was his palette: a slim board with two inkwells and a slot for reed pens. He chewed the end of a reed into a little brush, dipped it in water and rubbed it on the ink cake. Black ink was for the text. Red ink was for titles and for corrections. Marking mistakes in red is a very, very old habit.

cards.headline: Worth the homework
cards.body: Why put up with years of copying? Because most Egyptians could not read or write, a scribe automatically ranked above most people. Egyptian texts didn’t hide the boast either: the scribe gave the orders, they said, while the rest did the work. It’s quite a sales pitch for school.

title: Egyptian Math
objective: After this level you can explain how Egyptians wrote numbers and measured land.
summary: Egyptians repeated signs for 1, 10, 100 and 1,000, used unit fractions, and solved practical problems in the Rhind papyrus. Land lost to the river was measured for tax.

cards.headline: If the Nile swept away part of your field, did you still owe the full tax?
cards.body: Herodotus heard the Egyptian answer: no. But proving it took numbers, fractions and careful measuring.

cards.headline: Counting with pictures
cards.body: Egyptians counted in tens, like you do, with a separate sign for 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and on up: a stroke, a cattle hobble, a coil of rope, a lotus flower. To write a number, you repeated each sign as many times as needed, so 300 was three coils of rope. Simple to read, but writing 999 took 27 signs.
cards.callout: 1 stroke · 10 hobble · 100 rope · 1,000 lotus

cards.headline: Only one on top
cards.body: Fractions came with a rule: use unit fractions, the kind with 1 on top, like a half or a third. Need five-sixths? Write a half plus a third. The one big exception was two-thirds. The Rhind papyrus, now in the British Museum, opens with a long table of fractions to help with division, then works through 84 problems. It was copied in the 17th century BCE from a text about two centuries older.

cards.headline: Measuring what the river took
cards.body: The Rhind problems are practical: sharing bread and beer as wages, working out the area of fields. Land mattered because of Level 2’s flood. Herodotus heard that a man who lost part of his field to the river could report it. The king sent men to measure how much was gone, and the tax shrank to match. Herodotus thought the Greeks learned land measuring from Egypt. Math, it turns out, started as a tax dispute.

title: The Calendar
objective: After this level you can explain Egypt’s 365-day calendar and the rising of Sirius.
summary: Egypt’s civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days, grouped into the three seasons, plus 5 extra days: 365 in all. Sirius’s rising marked New Year, and without leap years the calendar drifted.

cards.headline: Egypt’s calendar had 365 days. Its New Year still wandered off.
cards.body: Egyptians made the first known calendar with a 365-day year, very close to the real solar year. Very close, but not quite, and a bright star kept score.

cards.headline: Tidy math, one bright star
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s three seasons, Akhet, Peret and Shemu, each four months long? That’s 12 months, and every month had exactly 30 days: 360 in all. Five extra days at the end made 365. The New Year was signaled by Sirius, which Egyptians called Sothis. Each year it first rose just before sunrise at about the time the flood began. Egyptians long believed the star caused the flood.

mascot.line: A quarter of a day sounds harmless. Give it a few centuries.

cards.body: There was a catch. Sirius came back every 365.25 days, not 365. With no leap year, the calendar slipped a quarter of a day every year, a whole day every four years. title: Medicine
objective: After this level you can describe Egyptian medicine and the medical papyri.
summary: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is a chiefly practical casebook of 48 injuries with honest verdicts; the Ebers Papyrus mixes hundreds of remedies and spells with an early description of the heart.

cards.headline: An Egyptian casebook sorted injuries three ways: treat, fight, or let be.
cards.body: Egyptian doctors wrote down what they knew on papyrus. Two famous scrolls survive, and they show two very different sides of Egyptian medicine.

cards.headline: The surgeon’s casebook
cards.body: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, from about 1600 BCE and written in hieratic, describes 48 cases of injuries, mostly to the head, neck and upper body. Every case follows the same pattern: the injury, a diagnosis, a prognosis, then the treatment. And each gives a verdict: a condition the doctor will treat, one he will contend with, or one that cannot be treated. It is honest about its limits.

cards.headline: Almost no magic, until you turn it over
cards.body: The injury cases are chiefly practical, with treatments such as bandaging and splinting, and only one incantation. Flip the scroll over, though, and the back holds magical spells and recipes, including one “for making an old man into a youth.” Even a careful casebook had a wishful back page.

mascot.line: History, not a prescription. Please keep your crocodile bites for a modern doctor.

cards.headline: The remedy book
cards.body: The Ebers Papyrus, from about 1550 BCE, is a different kind of book: hundreds of magical formulas and folk remedies, for troubles from crocodile bites to toenail pain. Yet it also describes the heart as the center of the blood supply, with vessels running throughout the body. Spells and sharp observation sat side by side, on the same scroll.

title: Stars and Buildings
objective: After this level you can explain how Egyptians used the stars to line up buildings.
summary: Egyptians used star-sighting tools like the merkhet to lay out buildings. One leading idea says pyramid builders found north by lining up two stars on a plumb line.

cards.headline: The Great Pyramid’s sides face north, south, east and west, and accurately.
cards.body: How do you find true north for a building that size? Egyptians had tools for reading the night sky, and one leading idea says two stars did the job.

cards.headline: A star-watching kit
cards.body: Egyptians had instruments for the night sky. The merkhet was a bar with a plumb line hanging from it, used to measure stars as they crossed the sky. The bay was a forked stick for lining things up. A string, a weight and a stick: simple tools, pointed at the stars.
cards.callout: Merkhet: bar + plumb line. Bay: forked stick.

mascot.line: The mistakes turned out to be the best clue. I love it when that happens.

cards.headline: Two stars and a plumb line
cards.body: In the pyramid age, no star marked the north pole of the sky. In 2000, Cambridge Egyptologist Kate Spence suggested a trick: watch two stars, Kochab and Mizar, circle that empty spot, and wait until a plumb line lines them both up. Then you are looking north. The clincher: the small errors in earlier and later pyramids follow the slow drift of those same two stars.

cards.headline: Stretching the cord
cards.body: Temples began with a ceremony. Temple reliefs show the king performing “stretching the cord,” a surveying rite, together with Seshat, the goddess of writing. Measuring out a building and writing shared a goddess. In Egypt, knowing things and building things went together.

title: Stories on Tomb Walls
objective: After this level you can explain what tomb paintings show about Egyptian life.
summary: Nebamun’s tomb paintings show a scribe’s ideal life: hunting with his cat, his herds counted, his fields assessed. They show how he wished to be remembered, not how most lived.

cards.headline: About 1350 BCE, a scribe went bird hunting with his cat. You can still watch.
cards.body: The scene is painted on his tomb wall, and it’s now in the British Museum. Tomb paintings are one of our best windows into Egyptian life, as long as you remember whose life they show.

cards.headline: Nebamun in the marshes
cards.body: Nebamun was a scribe in charge of grain at Thebes. In his painting he stands on a small papyrus boat, a throw-stick in one hand and three herons in the other. His wife stands behind him and his daughter sits below. His cat pounces on birds startled out of the reeds. It’s a perfect day out, painted to last forever.

cards.headline: The estate at work
cards.body: Other scenes show Nebamun’s estate. Scribes write down his geese and cattle as they are driven past. Inspectors check a grain field to assess it for tax. Remember Level 43’s scribes and Level 44’s tax measurers? Here they are, on the job, in paint.

cards.headline: The highlight reel
cards.body: Why paint all this? The pictures recorded how Nebamun wanted to be remembered, and the life he hoped to have in the afterlife. So they’re idealised. And only the wealthy paid for tomb paintings, so they don’t show how most Egyptians lived. Think of them as a highlight reel, not a home video.

title: Jewelry and Glass
objective: After this level you can describe Egyptian jewelry, faience and glass.
summary: Egyptian jewelry paired gold with carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli, or with glassy materials made to imitate them: faience from about 4000 BCE, glass from about 1500 BCE.

cards.headline: Egypt’s jewelry came in gold and three colors. Some of the colors were man-made.
cards.body: The colors could come from stones dug out of the ground, or from Egyptian workshops. Here’s how a craft learned to make them.

cards.headline: Gold and three colors
cards.body: In Egyptian jewelry, gold dominates. It is usually set with three colors of stone: carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli. They went into diadems, necklaces, pectorals, amulets, bracelets, earrings and rings. And the designs were mostly symbols with precise names and meanings, closely linked to hieroglyphic writing. A necklace could carry a message.

cards.headline: Color from a workshop
cards.body: Jewelers didn’t always use real stones: they often used glassy pastes that imitated them. The oldest was faience, made in Egypt from about 4000 BCE from silica, soda and lime, with a little copper or cobalt for color. Faience and glass went into objects wanted by all levels of society, not just pharaohs. Everyone could shine a little.

cards.headline: Glass arrives late
cards.body: Glass came much later, in the New Kingdom, about 1500 BCE. It took two stages: first the raw glass was made, then it was reheated and shaped. That means Egyptians were making faience for some 2,500 years before they made glass. Patience, or just very good faience.
