title: Homes of Mud Brick
objective: After this level you can describe Egyptian houses and how they kept cool.
summary: Egyptians built homes, and even palaces, of sun-dried Nile mud brick and kept stone for tombs and temples. High windows and roof vents kept houses cool.

cards.headline: Egypt built its gods houses of stone and its people houses of mud.
cards.body: That choice is why you can still walk into an Egyptian temple but will struggle to find an ordinary Egyptian’s front door. Here’s what homes were made of, and how they beat the heat.

cards.headline: Bricks from the riverbank
cards.body: An Egyptian house began as Nile mud: a mix of clay and sand, sometimes with bits of straw or animal droppings stirred in. Workers pressed it into rectangular molds and left the bricks to dry in the sun. No kiln needed. Mud brick and wood were the standard building materials for houses throughout Egyptian history, and even royal palaces were mud brick. The river that fed you also built your walls.

mascot.line: Built to last forever, or built to live in today. Egyptians knew exactly which was which.

cards.headline: Stone was for forever
cards.body: From the Old Kingdom on, stone went into tombs, the eternal homes of the dead, and temples, the eternal homes of the gods. Mud brick was for the living. There’s a second reason homes vanished: most towns stood in the cultivated, flooded valley, while temples and tombs were built on ground the flood didn’t reach. Remember Level 3’s red land, whose dry climate made it ideal for cemeteries? The dead got the better real estate.

cards.headline: Built to beat the heat
cards.body: Inside, the goal was shade and moving air. Windows sat high in the walls to cut down the sunlight, and hooded vents on the roof caught the breeze and let it into the house. A rich home could be huge: the house of the vizier Nakht at Tell el-Amarna had at least 30 rooms, with separate apartments for Nakht, his family and his guests, plus bathrooms and lavatories. Air conditioning, Egyptian style: a scoop on the roof.
cards.callout: High windows keep the sun out; roof vents let the breeze in.

title: Bread and Beer
objective: After this level you can describe what Egyptians ate and drank.
summary: Bread and beer, both made from grain, were Egypt’s staples. Beer was thick and nourishing, food rations served as pay, and sandy bread wore down people’s teeth.

cards.headline: Ask an ancient Egyptian what’s for dinner. Bread. And beer.
cards.body: Every day. Bread and beer were the staples of the Egyptian diet, and both came from the same grain. Here’s why beer counted as food, and why bread came with a price.

cards.headline: Same grain, two jobs
cards.body: Remember the emmer wheat and barley from Level 4? That grain became bread and beer, the staples of the diet. Bread was made mainly with emmer, baked as flat loaves a bit like pita or as tall cones. Beer used basically the same ingredients, so baking and brewing went hand in hand. The farming year ended at the dinner table.

cards.headline: Beer was a meal
cards.body: Forget a crisp lager. Egyptian beer was thick and cloudy, probably weaker than modern beer, and an important source of nutrition rather than just a treat. And since Egypt didn’t use coins or paper money, food doubled as pay: workers and household staff were often paid in rations. Payday smelled like a bakery.

cards.headline: A bakery in miniature
cards.body: Remember Meketre, whose model boat you met in Level 5? His tomb also held a model bakery and brewery, made about 1981 to 1975 BCE and now at the Met. Tiny men crush grain with pestles, women grind it into flour, and a basket of cone-shaped loaves waits in the middle. Bread and beer shared one workshop because they shared one set of ingredients.

mascot.line: Imagine a little sand in every bite, every day, for life. Your teeth would notice too.

cards.headline: The gritty truth
cards.body: That flour came with extras. Heavy tooth wear is the most common dental problem found in ancient Egyptian remains, and experts blame a coarse diet made even rougher by sand, mostly blown in on the wind, that ended up in the bread. Every loaf was a little bit of sandpaper. Egypt’s favorite food slowly ate Egypt’s teeth.

title: Linen and Eye Paint
objective: After this level you can explain Egyptian clothes and why both men and women wore makeup.
summary: Egyptians dressed in linen woven from flax. Men and women both wore green and black eye paint, for beauty, the gods and health; a 2010 lab study hints it may have helped fight infection.

cards.headline: In ancient Egypt, men wore eyeliner too. And they had reasons.
cards.body: Cosmetics were worn by both sexes, and the eyes got the most attention. The clothes were simple. The makeup may have done more than look good.

cards.headline: Dressed in flax
cards.body: Level 4’s flax crop ended up on people’s backs. Linen, woven from flax, was Egypt’s chief textile; wool was used more rarely, for things like warm cloaks. Men wore a short skirt tied at the waist. Women wore a sheath-like gown that ran from the ankles to just below the breasts. Light cloth for a hot country: the dress code was basically “linen, and not much of it.”

cards.headline: Green and black
cards.body: Egyptians wore green eye shadow made from powdered malachite and black or gray eyeliner. One ingredient of dark eye paint was galena, a lead sulfide mineral. Why bother? Egyptians thought eye paint looked good and pleased the gods, and they also believed it was healthy: it was said to keep off disease-carrying flies and block the sun’s glare. Beauty, religion and sunglasses in one.

mascot.line: A skin cell in a dish isn’t an eye. Good science says “maybe” when it means maybe.

cards.headline: What the lab found
cards.body: In 2010, French chemists tested lead compounds from Egyptian makeup on human skin cells in the lab. The compounds raised the cells’ output of nitric oxide, which helps the immune system fight bacteria, by up to 240 percent. That hints the makeup could have helped against eye infections. It isn’t proof it worked on real eyes, and lead is toxic: today the US FDA warns that lead-containing kohl can cause lead poisoning.

title: Growing Up in Egypt
objective: After this level you can describe childhood and schooling in ancient Egypt.
summary: Children wore the sidelock of youth. Only elite children had a chance at schooling; most learned by apprenticeship, and fingerprints show children as young as ten working in workshops.

cards.headline: How do you know a child worked in an ancient workshop? Check the fingerprints.
cards.body: Egyptian children left their marks in clay, in art and even in their hairstyles. Here’s what growing up by the Nile looked like.

cards.headline: The hairstyle of childhood
cards.body: In Egyptian art you can spot a child at a glance. Children were often shown unclothed, with a single plait of hair hanging at the side of the head: the sidelock of youth, also called the Horus lock. Many are drawn with a finger to the mouth, sucking a thumb. Egyptian artists used a simple code: one braid, no clothes, thumb in mouth.

cards.headline: School for the few
cards.body: Most children never sat in a classroom. Only children from elite and royal families had the chance of some schooling. Everyone else learned by apprenticeship, watching and helping an adult at work. Girls’ education centred on home life, learned from their mothers. For most kids, the classroom was the kitchen, the field or the workshop.

mascot.line: A fingerprint in clay: the closest thing archaeology has to a child’s signature.

cards.headline: Small hands at work
cards.body: Children worked from a young age to help support their families. One job was pressing amulets into lumps of clay to make moulds. Fingerprints left in those moulds show that children as young as ten were working in workshops. And work meant pay the Egyptian way: in a land without coins, workers were often paid in food rations. Their work still carries their fingerprints.

title: Women's Rights
objective: After this level you can explain the legal rights Egyptian women had.
summary: Egyptian women could own and sell property, make contracts and go to court in their own name, as Naunakhte’s will shows. But equal in law was not equal in life.

cards.headline: An Egyptian mother cut some of her children out of her will. The law let her.
cards.body: Her name was Naunakhte, and her will survives on papyrus. It shows something unusual for the ancient world: a woman with legal rights of her own.

cards.headline: Equal on paper
cards.body: From the Old Kingdom on, an Egyptian woman’s formal legal status was nearly identical to a man’s, married or not. She could buy, own and sell property in her own name, make contracts, take someone to court or be sued, and act as a witness. She didn’t need a man to represent her. Britannica puts it a notch lower: her status was “only marginally inferior” to a man’s. Either way, that was rare in the ancient world.

cards.headline: Naunakhte’s will
cards.body: Naunakhte lived in Deir el-Medina, the tomb builders’ village you’ll visit in Level 59. In old age she set out which of her children would inherit from her, and left out the ones who hadn’t cared for her or supported her. Her property was hers to divide, completely separate from her husband’s. Look after your mother: in Egypt, it could be a legal matter.

mascot.line: Rights on paper matter. So does who actually gets to use them.

cards.headline: Equal in law, not in life
cards.body: Don’t picture equality, though. Socially, men and women were not equal. Women seldom held paid public posts, so they usually earned less and depended on family, which could leave them worse off if a marriage ended. Even though the law allowed it, women rarely served as witnesses to legal documents. Egyptian women had rights on paper that most ancient women never had. Daily life still ran on men’s terms.

title: Cats and Other Pets
objective: After this level you can explain why cats were so loved in Egypt.
summary: Cats guarded Egypt’s grain from rodents and snakes, lived as pets and were linked to the goddess Bastet. Greek visitors reported families shaving their eyebrows when a cat died.

cards.headline: Egyptians called a cat “miu.” Say it out loud.
cards.body: The word meant “he or she who mews”: a cat named for its meow. Egyptians loved cats for good practical reasons and good religious ones.

cards.headline: Hired for pest control
cards.body: Cats earned their place. They hunted the rodents that threatened to eat Egypt’s grain and spread disease, and they killed dangerous animals like snakes and scorpions. Pest control was the main reason cats were domesticated at all. A storeroom of Level 4’s wheat and barley needed a guard, and the guard purred. Art shows the rest of the story: cats in collars, lurking under chairs, just like yours.

cards.headline: A goddess with whiskers
cards.body: Cats also had a goddess. Bastet was worshipped first as a lioness and later as a cat, often shown as a woman with a cat’s head. She watched over the home, fertility, joy and the protection of children. Her home city was Bubastis in the Nile Delta, and people wore little cat figures as amulets, probably because of her. From fierce lioness to house cat: Bastet got tamer, just like her animals.

mascot.line: No eyebrows meant “our cat just died.” Everyone in the street would know.

cards.headline: Mourning the family cat
cards.body: Losing a cat hurt. Herodotus, the Greek traveler you met in Level 2, wrote that when a cat died, everyone in the household shaved their eyebrows. For a dog, they shaved their heads and whole bodies. Diodorus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, wrote that he saw an Egyptian crowd kill a Roman who had accidentally killed a cat. These are outsiders’ reports, but they agree: in Egypt, you did not mess with the cat.

title: Games and Music
objective: After this level you can describe board games like senet and Egyptian music.
summary: Senet, played on 30 squares with throwing sticks, was one of the oldest board games; rich and poor both played it. Harps, flutes, singers and the sistrum filled festivals and temples with music.

cards.headline: Egyptians were playing board games more than 5,000 years ago.
cards.body: Their favorite, senet, is one of the earliest board games known. Here’s how it was played, who played it and what music was playing in the background.

cards.headline: How to play senet
cards.body: Senet was played on a board of 30 squares, in three rows of ten. Two players each got the same number of pieces, usually five to seven, and raced them to the end. Instead of dice, they threw casting sticks or bones. The last squares were special: one marked “good” gave a free turn, and a water hazard knocked a piece off the board. Evidence suggests Egyptians were playing it as early as about 3100 BCE.

cards.headline: A game for everyone
cards.body: Senet wasn’t just for palaces. The wealthy played on ornate boards, while people with less scratched a grid onto stone, a table or the floor. Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertari were fans. In the New Kingdom the game, whose name means “passing,” became linked with the journey to the afterlife. Another early game, mehen, used a spiral board shaped like a coiled snake, with lion-shaped pieces. Its rules are lost, so nobody has won it in a very long time.

mascot.line: Senet on the floor, a harp in the corner: an Egyptian game night had a soundtrack.

cards.headline: Music at the party
cards.body: Music filled festivals, banquets, funerals and temple rituals. The most common band was harps, flutes and singers. In temples, especially in the worship of the goddess Hathor, musicians shook the sistrum: a rattle with loose crossbars, often hung with jingles. Picture the scene: a harp, a flute, a singer and a sacred rattle keeping the beat.

title: Work and Trades
objective: After this level you can describe the work of farmers, builders and craftsmen.
summary: Nearly all Egyptians farmed, while skilled craftspeople worked beside them and were paid in rations. The Satire of the Trades mocked every job except the scribe’s.

cards.headline: An Egyptian father’s advice: be a scribe, since every other job is miserable.
cards.body: Egyptologists call it the Satire of the Trades, and New Kingdom students copied it as a writing exercise. It’s a biased guide to Egyptian work, and a very vivid one.

cards.headline: The Satire of the Trades
cards.body: In this text, a father walks his son to scribal school and mocks every other job on the way. The potter is covered with earth. The barber wears out his arms. The fisherman works among crocodiles. The washerman handles other people’s filth. It probably dates to the Middle Kingdom, and students kept copying it for centuries after. Career counseling, Egyptian style: scare the kid into studying.

cards.headline: Most people farmed
cards.body: The jokes hide a plain fact: nearly all Egyptians worked the land and were probably tied to it. In theory all land belonged to the king, though people living on it couldn’t easily be removed, and some land could be bought and sold. So most Egyptians lived by Level 4’s farming year: Akhet’s flood, Peret’s plowing and sowing, Shemu’s harvest. The river set everyone’s work calendar.

mascot.line: Every job has a bad side. This text just wrote them all down in one place.

cards.headline: Craft and pay
cards.body: Craftspeople worked alongside the farmers, and Britannica says they raised their techniques, many first borrowed from Asia, to extraordinary levels of perfection. With no coins, pay often came as food rations, just as Level 52 described. As for the Satire, some Egyptologists doubt “satire” is even the right word, because its pictures of hard labor are so starkly realistic. The joke may have been truer than it was funny.

title: The Village of Tomb Builders
objective: After this level you can describe the workers’ village of Deir el-Medina.
summary: Deir el-Medina housed the craftsmen who built the royal tombs. Its tens of thousands of documents record absences for brewing beer and, under Ramesses III, the first recorded strike.

cards.headline: “Absent: brewing beer.” An Egyptian work register really says that.
cards.body: It comes from a village of tomb builders whose everyday notes survive by the tens of thousands. Here’s the best window we have into ordinary Egyptian lives.

cards.headline: The village of the tomb builders
cards.body: Deir el-Medina was a New Kingdom village of the craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings, and their families. It’s special because of its paperwork: researchers have recovered tens of thousands of written documents, most from about 1275 to 1075 BCE. In some periods most men there could read and write, when literacy across Egypt is estimated at only about 1 or 2 percent. A village of workmen, with a library’s worth of notes.

cards.headline: Notes on stone
cards.body: For everyday notes, villagers wrote on ostraca: flakes of limestone and pieces of broken pottery, an alternative to papyrus. One, now in the British Museum, lists workmen’s absences over 280 days of Year 40 of Ramesses II. The reasons include illness, embalming a relative and brewing beer. Remember Level 52? Beer was food, so brewing it was a real excuse.

mascot.line: The first recorded strike was a sit-in. Some protest tactics are very, very old.

cards.headline: The first recorded strike
cards.body: In Year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1157 BCE, the workmen’s grain rations were late. So they stopped work, shouted “We are hungry!” and sat down behind a temple. The grain came, and later the protests started again. The scribe Amunnakht wrote it all down on a papyrus now in Turin. It’s the first recorded strike in history. When your pay is food, a late payday means a hungry family.
cards.callout: The first recorded strike: late rations, empty stomachs, tools down.

title: Checkpoint: Daily Life
objective: After this level you can describe home, food, work and fun in ancient Egypt.
summary: Kings carved their deeds in stone; ordinary Egyptians left clues. Teeth, fingerprints, lost towns and the everyday writing of Deir el-Medina show how people lived.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: how do we know what ordinary Egyptians ate, did and loved?
cards.body: Kings carved their deeds in stone. Everyone else left clues: teeth, fingerprints, scraps of pottery. Time to play detective with this chapter’s evidence.

cards.headline: Clues nobody meant to leave
cards.body: Some evidence was never meant as a record. Worn-down teeth show that Egyptian bread was gritty with sand. Fingerprints in clay moulds show children as young as ten at work in workshops. Even what’s missing is a clue: ordinary homes mostly vanished because towns stood in the flooded valley, while temples and tombs stood where the flood couldn’t reach.

mascot.line: No single clue tells the story. Line them up, and ordinary Egyptians start to talk.

cards.headline: Clues people wrote down
cards.body: Then there’s writing, and the tomb builders’ village is our richest source: its papyri and ostraca show details of daily life rarely seen anywhere else in Egypt. A limestone flake lists a worker absent for brewing beer. A papyrus records hungry workmen striking over late rations. Naunakhte’s will cuts out children who didn’t care for her. Outsiders add their own notes, like Herodotus on families shaving their eyebrows for a dead cat. Put together, you meet a people who worked hard, ate bread, drank beer and loved their cats.

title: The Hyksos
objective: After this level you can explain who the Hyksos were and what they brought to Egypt.
summary: The Hyksos, “rulers of foreign lands,” held northern Egypt from Avaris and brought the horse and chariot. Ahmose of Thebes drove them out and began the New Kingdom.

cards.headline: For about a century, northern Egypt was ruled by kings from abroad.
cards.body: Remember Level 1’s Intermediate Periods, when Egypt split apart? In the second one, the north ended up under foreign kings. How Egypt got rid of them is where the New Kingdom begins.

cards.headline: Rulers of foreign lands
cards.body: Egyptians called these kings heqa khasut, “rulers of foreign lands,” and the Greek form of that title gives us “Hyksos.” For generations, people from Southwest Asia had been settling in the eastern Delta. As the pharaohs’ grip weakened, leaders at their city of Avaris rose to power and ruled much of Lower Egypt as the 15th Dynasty. Many scholars now think it was less a sudden invasion than the neighbors slowly taking over the street.
cards.callout: Heqa khasut: “rulers of foreign lands”

cards.headline: New weapons
cards.body: The Hyksos brought new technology to Egypt: the horse and chariot, the composite bow and improved metal weapons. Egypt kept the chariot and the composite bow after the Hyksos were gone, and those two advantages would later help it build an empire. The Hyksos kings left, but their chariots stayed.

mascot.line: Villains in the later stories, kings in the paperwork. It pays to read both.

cards.headline: The fightback from Thebes
cards.body: The fightback came from Thebes, in the south. King Kamose campaigned against the Hyksos, and his successor Ahmose captured Avaris and drove them out. Ahmose founded the 18th Dynasty, and with it the New Kingdom, around 1550 BCE. Later Egyptian texts cast the Hyksos as villains, yet they had ruled as pharaohs and appear as legitimate kings in the Turin king list.

title: An Egyptian Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt built an empire in the New Kingdom.
summary: After the Hyksos, New Kingdom kings built buffer zones in Nubia and Canaan that grew into an empire, reaching the Fourth Cataract and the Euphrates.

cards.headline: Egypt had learned a hard lesson: trouble next door can end up on your throne.
cards.body: Ahmose understood that the Hyksos had grown strong because earlier kings let them. So the New Kingdom’s pharaohs set out to keep the next threat a long way from home.

cards.headline: Buffer zones
cards.body: After the Hyksos were gone, Ahmose and the kings after him pushed Egypt’s borders outward, creating buffer zones: Nubia to the south, Canaan to the north. Later pharaohs, above all Thutmose III, grew those buffers into an empire. Think of a moat, except the moat is made of other countries.
cards.callout: Keep enemies far away, then keep what you took

cards.headline: Past the rapids
cards.body: Remember the First Cataract, the rapids at Aswan that marked Egypt’s southern border in Level 5? New Kingdom armies went far beyond it. Egypt conquered all of Nubia and held the Nile as far as the Fourth Cataract. The prize was gold from the Nubian deserts, and Egypt ran the region through viceroys who oversaw the collection of tribute.

cards.headline: To the Euphrates
cards.body: In the north, Thutmose I campaigned through Syria as far as the Euphrates River. For kings whose whole world had been one river valley, that was quite a road trip. A kingdom built on the Nile now touched a second great river, and Egypt was no longer just a country. It was an empire.

title: Karnak
objective: After this level you can describe the great temple complex at Karnak.
summary: Karnak at Thebes, Egypt’s largest temple complex, was the house of Amun-Re, “the Hidden One.” After the Hyksos and the empire, Amun’s temples grew rich.

cards.headline: One temple, nearly 2,000 years of building work.
cards.body: Ruler after ruler added something to Karnak, from the Middle Kingdom onward. So whose house was it, and who paid for all that stone?

cards.headline: The house of the Hidden One
cards.body: Karnak stands on the east bank of the Nile at Thebes, today’s Luxor. It is the largest temple complex in Egypt, the great temple of the state god Amun-Re. Amun’s name meant “the Hidden One,” and artists painted him blue to show that he was invisible. An invisible god, with the biggest house in the country.

cards.headline: Paid for by victory
cards.body: Amun was the god of Thebes, and Theban kings had just driven out the Hyksos (Level 61). After that victory, and the empire that followed, Amun’s standing and the wealth of his temples grew. From the New Kingdom on, Karnak was among the largest and wealthiest temples in the land. Win a war, thank your god, add a wing.

cards.headline: A forest of stone
cards.body: Karnak’s showpiece is the Great Hypostyle Hall, whose roof rested on 134 columns. It has been called one of the wonders of antiquity. Walking in is like wandering through a forest where every trunk is carved stone.

title: The Valley of the Kings
objective: After this level you can explain why pharaohs chose a hidden valley for their tombs.
summary: From Thutmose I, New Kingdom kings hid rock-cut tombs in a desert valley at Thebes under a pyramid-shaped peak, with temples built apart. Almost all were robbed anyway.

cards.headline: Pyramids told everyone where a king was buried. That was the problem.
cards.body: New Kingdom pharaohs, fearing for their rich burials, tried another plan: hide the tomb, and hope nobody finds it.

cards.headline: A lonely valley
cards.body: Thutmose I is thought to have been the first king to cut his tomb in the Valley of the Kings, a narrow valley in the western hills at Thebes, probably for security. Kings of the 18th, 19th and 20th Dynasties followed, hiding their rock-cut tombs out of sight. Remember Level 3’s red land? Its dry climate made the desert an ideal place for cemeteries.

mascot.line: A natural pyramid overhead and nothing to point at your door. Clever.

cards.headline: A pyramid after all
cards.body: Pharaohs didn’t give up on pyramids entirely. Above the valley rises a peak called the Qurn, whose shape may have reminded Egyptians of a pyramid. Their temples for worship after death were built separately, at the edge of the farmland, far from the hidden tombs. The tomb went into hiding; the temple stayed on show.

cards.headline: Built to baffle
cards.body: A typical tomb was a corridor sloping down into the rock, broken by deep shafts (perhaps to stop robbers, perhaps to catch floodwater), ending in a burial chamber. It didn’t work. Virtually every tomb in the valley was emptied in ancient times; Tutankhamun’s is the famous one that escaped. Hidden, it turns out, isn’t the same as safe.

title: Thutmose III
objective: After this level you can explain how Thutmose III expanded Egypt.
summary: Thutmose III won at Megiddo by a bold mountain route, fought 17 campaigns, raised conquered princes at court and turned buffer zones into an empire.

cards.headline: New York’s “Cleopatra’s Needle” has nothing to do with Cleopatra.
cards.body: The obelisk in Central Park, and its twin in London, were first set up by Thutmose III before the sun temple at Heliopolis, about 1,400 years before Cleopatra. So who was he?

cards.headline: A late start
cards.body: Thutmose III became king as a boy, around 1479 BCE. For years Hatshepsut ruled as king beside him, until her death in his 22nd year. Then, almost as soon as he ruled alone, he marched into the Levant. Twenty-two years is a long wait for your turn.

cards.headline: The narrow pass
cards.body: At Megiddo, Thutmose III passed up the safer roads and led his army along a narrow path over the mountain, surprising the enemy. After a siege of several months the city fell, and the spoils included hundreds of chariots and more than 2,000 horses. Remember the Hyksos’ chariots from Level 61? Now Egypt was collecting them by the hundred.

cards.headline: Holding an empire

And he had his campaigns carved on the walls of Amun’s temple at Karnak (Level 63). The buffer zones had become an empire.

title: Akhenaten and the Sun Disc
objective: After this level you can explain Akhenaten's religious revolution.
summary: Akhenaten raised the Aten, the sun disc, above Amun, built Akhetaten (Amarna) and erased Amun’s name. Whether it was monotheism is debated; it did not outlast him.

cards.headline: One pharaoh snubbed Egypt’s mightiest god and built a capital for another.
cards.body: His name was Akhenaten. Historians still argue about what exactly his new religion was.

cards.headline: The sun’s disc
cards.body: Amenhotep IV became king around 1352 BCE. He raised one god, the Aten, above almost all the others, mighty Amun included. The Aten wasn’t drawn as a person: it was the disc of the sun itself, bathing the king in its rays. The king even changed his name to Akhenaten, “beneficial to the Aten.”

cards.headline: A city and a chisel
cards.body: He built a new capital on empty ground on the east bank of the Nile: Akhetaten, “Horizon of the Aten,” known today as Amarna. From his fifth year, he set out to erase Amun’s name and image from monuments, wrecking parts of many temples. Remember Karnak from Level 63? Amun’s grand house was now a target.

mascot.line: Sometimes the most honest answer in history is “it depends on the word you pick.”

cards.headline: The first monotheist?
cards.body: Early Egyptologists hailed Akhenaten as the world’s first monotheist. Many scholars now prefer the word monolatry: worshipping one god in preference to all others. His Aten cult also drew on other gods. One god, or one overwhelming favorite? The debate goes on.

cards.headline: Undone
cards.body: The revolution didn’t outlive him. About four years after his death the court went back to Thebes, and Akhetaten was abandoned. Amun was restored as king of the gods, and the Aten religion quickly faded.

title: Nefertiti
objective: After this level you can describe Nefertiti's role and her famous portrait bust.
summary: Nefertiti, Akhenaten’s queen, appears in art with a royal role. Her bust was found at Amarna in 1912; whether she later ruled as co-regent is debated.

cards.headline: Nefertiti’s famous bust has only one inlaid eye. Nobody knows for certain why.
cards.body: That missing eye is just one of the mysteries around Akhenaten’s queen.

cards.headline: Beside the king
cards.body: Nefertiti was Akhenaten’s queen, and she was never in the background. She worshipped the Aten alongside him and was shown at the same scale as the king. Some scenes even show her smiting Egypt’s enemies, a motif previously reserved for the pharaoh. Her name is usually translated “a beautiful woman has come.”

cards.headline: The bust
cards.body: On 6 December 1912, a German team led by Ludwig Borchardt found a painted limestone bust of Nefertiti at Amarna, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose. It is now in the Neues Museum in Berlin. Only the right eye has an inlay, and many think the bust was a model kept in the workshop for sculptors to copy. A masterpiece that may have been a reference sheet.
cards.callout: Found in a sculptor’s workshop, not a tomb

mascot.line: When the clues run out, “we don’t know yet” is a perfectly good answer.

cards.headline: Queen, co-ruler or king?
cards.body: What Nefertiti did later is one of Egypt’s great debates. Some scholars think she ruled beside Akhenaten as co-regent, or even as king under another name. Others disagree, and the evidence is not conclusive. The face everyone recognizes belongs to a woman nobody can fully place.

title: The Voyage to Punt
objective: After this level you can describe Egypt's trade expeditions to the land of Punt.
summary: Egypt sailed the Red Sea to Punt for incense, gold, leopard skins and baboons, carrying ships across the desert. Punt’s location is still debated.

cards.headline: Egypt sailed to a land of incense and gold. Nobody knows exactly where.
cards.body: Egyptians called it Punt, and they went to remarkable lengths to get there.

cards.headline: The wonders of Punt
cards.body: From Punt, Egyptian expeditions brought back incense, gold, leopard skins and even living baboons. Voyages there are recorded at least as early as about 2200 BCE, under Pepi II. The most famous one, sent by Hatshepsut, was carved on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahri. It was a shopping trip worth writing on a temple.

cards.headline: Flat-pack ships
cards.body: Getting there took ingenuity. At Wadi Gawasis on the Red Sea coast, archaeologists found that Egyptians built ships by the Nile, took them apart, carried them across the desert and put them back together on the shore. Caves there held ship timbers, rope and cargo boxes labeled “wonders of Punt,” from roughly 4,000 years ago. Flat-pack furniture, but make it a seagoing ship.

cards.headline: So where was it?
cards.body: Punt lay somewhere around the southern Red Sea, and scholars have argued over it for more than 150 years. The leading candidates include the Horn of Africa and southern Arabia. One clue came from baboon mummies: chemical signatures in two New Kingdom baboons point to Eritrea, Ethiopia or Somalia. The researchers call the result provisional.

title: Letters in Clay
objective: After this level you can explain what the Amarna letters show about ancient diplomacy.
summary: The Amarna Letters, 382 cuneiform tablets in Akkadian, show great kings writing to the pharaoh as “brother” and vassals bowing and pleading for attention.

cards.headline: Egypt’s royal mail wasn’t written in Egyptian.
cards.body: In 1887 a local woman at Tell el-Amarna, the site of Akhenaten’s old capital, stumbled on a cache of clay tablets. They turned out to be letters between the pharaoh and the rulers of his world.

cards.headline: A borrowed language
cards.body: There are 382 known Amarna tablets. They are cuneiform tablets written mostly in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the day, and they date to the reigns of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten. International diplomacy had a common language, and it wasn’t Egyptian.
cards.callout: Clay, cuneiform, Akkadian

cards.headline: Dear brother
cards.body: The great kings of Babylonia, Assyria, Mitanni and the Hittites wrote to the pharaoh as equals and called him “brother.” Their letters fuss over gifts and royal marriages. Tushratta, king of Mitanni, complained that gold statues he’d been promised arrived as gold-plated wood. Even brothers checked whether the gold was solid.

cards.headline: Seven times and seven times
cards.body: Egypt’s vassals in Syria and Canaan wrote very differently. The ruler of Gezer opened: “I fall at the feet of the king, my lord, my god, my Sun, seven times and seven times.” Vassal letters are full of local troubles and complaints that Egypt isn’t paying attention. This is Level 62’s empire, seen from the other end.

title: Tutankhamun
objective: After this level you can explain why a minor king became the most famous pharaoh.
summary: Tutankhamun became king as a child, turned Egypt back to the old gods and died at about 19. His small tomb largely escaped robbers, and its gold made him famous.

cards.headline: A boy king with “little claim to fame” became the most famous pharaoh.
cards.body: Britannica says it plainly: but for his tomb, Tutankhamun has little claim to fame. Yet he is better known than the longer-lived, better-documented kings before and after him. How does that happen?

cards.headline: A child on the throne
cards.body: Tutankhamun became king at about nine, around 1333 BCE, in the New Kingdom. He was born Tutankhaten, a name that included the Aten, the god of Akhenaten’s religious revolution. Under the boy king, Egypt turned back: a decree restored the temples, images, priests and privileges of the old gods. His name changed too, to Tutankhamun, now including Amun. New government, new name tag.

mascot.line: Three thousand years on, and the doctors are still arguing. That’s a very long second opinion.

cards.headline: A case still open
cards.body: Around 1323 BCE, at about 19, he died, and nobody knows for sure why. A 2010 study found malaria parasites in his mummy and suggested malaria combined with a bone disease. Others point to a badly broken leg. Neither diagnosis is certain, so the most famous mummy in the world still has an open file.

cards.headline: Famous for what nobody stole
cards.body: His tomb was small, hastily converted for him, and later hidden under rock chippings from a later tomb. It became the only royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings to largely escape the robbers. Inside, his mummy lay in a nest of three coffins, the innermost of solid gold, wearing a golden portrait mask, with more than 5,000 objects around him. Tutankhamun isn’t famous for what he did. He’s famous for what survived.
cards.callout: Short reign, small tomb, surviving gold

title: Ramesses the Great
objective: After this level you can explain why Ramesses II is remembered as a great builder.
summary: Ramesses II reigned for 66 years and put up more monuments and statues than any other pharaoh, recarving older statues as his own.

cards.headline: A famous poem made Ramesses II the symbol of forgotten power.
cards.body: Shelley’s sonnet “Ozymandias,” published in 1818, describes a ruined statue of Ramesses II, its boastful inscription standing in empty desert. The irony: few pharaohs ever worked harder at being remembered.

cards.headline: Sixty-six years
cards.body: Ramesses II, son of Seti I, reigned from 1279 to 1213 BCE: 66 years, one of the longest reigns in Egyptian history. He had more than 100 children and outlived many of them. Anyone younger than about 66 at his death had never known another king. That’s a lot of time to build.

cards.headline: The builder king
cards.body: And build he did: the Ramesseum, his great temple at Thebes; two temples at Abu Simbel; a new capital called Per-Ramessu; and work on Karnak’s Hypostyle Hall and at Abydos. He put up more monuments and statues than any other pharaoh. Walk around Egypt today and his face keeps turning up.
cards.callout: More monuments and statues than any other pharaoh

mascot.line: Ancient Egypt’s most prolific builder was also its most confident autographer.

cards.headline: Ramesses was here
cards.body: Not all of it was new. A statue in Turin’s Museo Egizio was made for an earlier king, probably Amenhotep II. Ramesses’ sculptors recarved its face to look like his official portrait and put his name on its belt. If you couldn’t build it, you could still sign it.

title: Abu Simbel
objective: After this level you can describe the temples of Abu Simbel and how they were moved.
summary: Ramesses II carved two temples into the cliffs at Abu Simbel. In the 1960s, a UNESCO-led campaign cut them into blocks and rebuilt them above the rising lake of the Aswan High Dam.

cards.headline: Twice a year, sunrise reaches the back of a temple cut deep into rock.
cards.body: At Abu Simbel, on about February 22 and October 22, the first rays of the morning sun run the whole length of Ramesses II’s great temple and light its innermost shrine. It still happens. Just not where the temple was built.

cards.headline: Four guards, all named Ramesses
cards.body: Ramesses built two temples at Abu Simbel. The great temple, for the sun gods Amon-Re and Re-Horakhte, has four seated figures of Ramesses at its entrance, each 20 metres tall. The smaller temple honors his queen, Nefertari, and the goddess Hathor, with 10.5-metre statues of king and queen. Visitors met the king four times before they got through the door.

cards.headline: A lake on the way
cards.body: Then came the Aswan High Dam, and its new reservoir was set to drown Abu Simbel. In 1960, UNESCO launched an international campaign to save the monuments of Nubia. Sun and sand the temples could handle. Water was another matter.

mascot.line: Ramesses built for eternity. Eternity needed some help from more than 50 countries.

cards.headline: Moving a mountain
cards.body: Between 1963 and 1968, engineers and scientists, funded by more than 50 countries, cut away the top of the cliff, sawed both temples into some 16,000 blocks and rebuilt them on high ground more than 60 metres above the old site. A jigsaw puzzle made of temple, reassembled uphill.

title: The Battle of Kadesh
objective: After this level you can explain the battle and the peace treaty that followed.
summary: At Kadesh, around 1274 BCE, Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw and advertised it as a victory. Years later the two powers signed the oldest peace treaty whose text survives.

cards.headline: Ramesses carved his great victory at Kadesh into temple walls. It wasn’t one.
cards.body: His reliefs show him single-handedly defeating the enemy. The battle was real, and so was the danger. It’s the ending that got edited.

cards.headline: Walking into a trap
cards.body: Around 1274 BCE, Ramesses marched into Syria to fight the Hittites, Egypt’s great rival, under their king Muwatallis, near the city of Kadesh on the Orontes River. Men posing as Hittite deserters fed him false information; they were enemy agents. A surprise Hittite attack scattered his army, in one of the largest chariot battles ever fought.

cards.headline: A draw, with good publicity
cards.body: Ramesses regrouped and counterattacked, and the day ended in what historians call an honorable draw. Neither side won outright, and Ramesses did not take Kadesh. Back home, though, he claimed a great victory, and his temple reliefs show him beating the enemy single-handed. Ancient spin, carved in stone.
cards.callout: What happened: a draw. What he carved: a victory.

mascot.line: Two old enemies, one treaty, and a copy right outside the room where nations still argue.

cards.headline: Peace, in writing
cards.body: Years later, Ramesses and a new Hittite king, Hattusili III, made peace. Theirs is the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives, made as between equal great powers, with the same promises on both sides: lasting peace, nonaggression, extradition and mutual help. Both versions survive: the Egyptian one on temple walls at Karnak, the Hittite one on a clay tablet from Hattusa. A replica hangs at the United Nations, near the Security Council.

title: Khufu
objective: After this level you can describe what we know about the builder of the Great Pyramid.
summary: Khufu built the Great Pyramid, yet few written sources about him remain. His only named statue is a 7.5 cm ivory figure, and Herodotus gave him a bad reputation that Egyptians did not share.

cards.headline: The Great Pyramid’s builder survives as a statue you could hide in your hand.

cards.headline: The man behind the pyramid
cards.body: Khufu, called Cheops by the Greeks, was the second king of the 4th Dynasty and the son of King Sneferu. He ruled in the Old Kingdom, the age of the great pyramids, and built the Great Pyramid at Giza. Yet few written sources about his life remain. We know his tomb far better than we know him.

mascot.line: Three weeks of sifting dirt for one tiny ivory head. Archaeology rewards patience.

cards.headline: Lost and found in the dirt
cards.body: The ivory statuette was found by Flinders Petrie at Abydos in 1903. It shows Khufu on a throne wearing the red crown of Lower Egypt (remember Level 6?). During the dig its head was knocked off and lost; three weeks later the team found it by sifting the excavated dirt. The builder of the Great Pyramid, rescued from a spoil heap by a sieve.

cards.headline: A bad review, two thousand years late
cards.body: Herodotus, the Greek historian from Level 2, wrote some 2,000 years after Khufu. He called the reigns of Khufu and his son Khafre 106 years of oppression and misery. Yet in Egypt itself, Khufu was remembered after his death as a wise ruler. Whose review would you trust: a visitor two thousand years late, or the people who kept his memory?

summary: Seti I, father of Ramesses II, built a temple at Abydos with some of Egypt’s finest reliefs and a selective list of kings, and a tomb decorated from end to end.

cards.headline: Ramesses the Great’s father may have been the better king.
cards.body: Scholars often rate Seti I above his far more famous son. He is far less famous, but he left some of the finest carving in any Egyptian temple.

cards.headline: Father of the Great
cards.body: Seti I, son of Ramesses I, reigned from about 1290 to 1279 BCE in the 19th Dynasty. He restored Egypt’s power abroad, fighting in Palestine and Syria and at least once against the Hittite king Muwatallis, the same enemy his son would meet at Kadesh. Then his son Ramesses II took the throne, and the spotlight.

mascot.line: Seventy-six kings made the cut. Tutankhamun didn’t. Fame is fickle.

cards.headline: The list with gaps
cards.body: At Abydos, Seti built a temple whose reliefs are among the finest in any Egyptian temple, many still with their original color. On one wall, Seti and his son Ramesses honor a list of 76 kings, from Menes, Level 8’s legendary first king, to Seti himself. But Hatshepsut, Akhenaten and Tutankhamun are missing. Remember Level 9’s warning that king lists leave out awkward rulers? Here’s one doing it.

cards.headline: Painted end to end
cards.body: Seti’s tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV17, is one of the longest there, and the first decorated with a complete program of religious texts. When Giovanni Belzoni found it in 1817, the paint still looked fresh. Seti’s alabaster sarcophagus now sits in Sir John Soane’s Museum in London.

title: Cleopatra
objective: After this level you can explain who Cleopatra was and how she ruled.
summary: Cleopatra VII came from a Macedonian Greek dynasty but learned Egyptian. She ruled from 51 to 30 BCE, allied with Caesar and Antony, and lost to Octavian.

cards.headline: Cleopatra came from a line of kings who never learned Egyptian.
cards.body: According to Plutarch, the kings before her hadn’t even tried. Cleopatra did. That tells you a lot about how she ruled.

cards.headline: Greek by family, Egyptian by choice
cards.body: Cleopatra VII was born in 70 or 69 BCE into the Ptolemies, a royal family of Macedonian Greek descent. Plutarch says she learned Egyptian and switched languages so easily that she seldom needed an interpreter. For political reasons she also styled herself the new Isis, after the Egyptian goddess. She didn’t just rule Egypt; she spoke to it.

cards.headline: A queen against Rome
cards.body: She ruled from 51 to 30 BCE. Forced out by her brother Ptolemy XIII, she regained power with Julius Caesar’s help and had a son by him, Caesarion. Later she allied with Mark Antony. In 31 BCE Octavian defeated them at the Battle of Actium, and in 30 BCE she died. Legend says by an asp’s bite; how she really died is uncertain. That same year, Egypt became a Roman province.
cards.callout: Caesar, Antony, Actium, 30 BCE

mascot.line: The most famous face in history, and her fans kept talking about her conversation.

cards.headline: What did she look like?
cards.body: Nobody knows for sure. A coin from her alliance with Antony shows both of them with beaked noses and jutting chins, like her Ptolemaic ancestors: a political image, not a photograph. Her mother isn’t known for certain, so part of her family tree is a question mark. And Plutarch wrote that her beauty alone wasn’t incomparable; her conversation was what charmed people.

title: The Pharaoh's Names
objective: After this level you can explain the royal names and the cartouche.
summary: A pharaoh had five names, four of them given at coronation. The throne name and birth name were written inside a cartouche, a rope loop standing for eternity.

cards.headline: A pharaoh didn’t have a name. He had five.
cards.body: One came at birth; the other four arrived with the crown. Two of them were drawn inside a loop of rope. And one of them became the title of a famous English poem.

cards.headline: Five names, five titles
cards.body: A pharaoh’s full title had five names, each introduced by a title: Horus, Two Ladies, Golden Horus, King of Upper and Lower Egypt, and Son of Re. Only one name was given at birth; the other four came at his coronation. “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” should ring a bell: Level 6 showed every king held it after unification. Becoming king meant getting a whole new name tag.

mascot.line: Spot an oval full of hieroglyphs, and you’ve found a royal name.

cards.headline: The rope loop
cards.body: Two of the names, the throne name and the birth name, were written inside an oval called a cartouche. It shows a loop of rope and stands for a shen ring, a circle symbolizing eternity, wrapped protectively around the king’s name. The word itself is French for a paper cartridge, which is what the ovals looked like. Eternity, mistaken for ammunition.
cards.callout: Cartouche = rope loop = eternity around a name

cards.headline: Names at work
cards.body: Names carried messages. Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun as Egypt went back to the old gods (Level 71). And Ramesses II’s throne name, Usermaatre, came out in Greek as “Ozymandias,” the king of Shelley’s poem (Level 72). The cartouche promised eternity; the pronunciation got lost in translation.

title: The Mummy's Curse
objective: After this level you can explain where the legend of the mummy's curse came from.
summary: When Lord Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in 1923, newspapers blamed a curse, a plot fiction had already written. A 2002 study found no evidence for it.

cards.headline: Tutankhamun’s tomb supposedly cursed its openers. Its excavator lived to 1939.
cards.body: Howard Carter, who led the excavation, died in London at 64. For a pharaoh’s revenge, that’s a remarkably slow start. So where did the curse come from?

cards.headline: One death, many headlines
cards.body: In April 1923, Lord Carnarvon, Carter’s patron, died in Cairo. The cause was an infection after a mosquito bite he got while visiting the newly opened burial chamber. His death set off sensational newspaper stories about a mummy’s curse. An infected bite is a sad story. A pharaoh’s revenge is a headline.
cards.callout: Real cause: an infected mosquito bite

cards.headline: The plot was already written
cards.body: The curse wasn’t new. Mummy curses had appeared in fiction long before: back in 1869, Louisa May Alcott published a thriller called “Lost in a Pyramid; or, The Mummy’s Curse.” When Carnarvon died, the story was waiting. The newspapers just had to fill in the names.

mascot.line: When a legend meets a spreadsheet, the spreadsheet usually wins.

cards.headline: Putting the curse on trial
cards.body: In 2002, a study in the BMJ, a medical journal, tested the legend. It compared Westerners who were exposed to the “curse” at the tomb with those who weren’t. The exposed group died at an average age of 70, and the difference was not significant. Verdict: no evidence of a curse. Mosquito, one. Pharaoh, zero.

title: The Sea Peoples
objective: After this level you can describe the raiders who struck around 1177 BCE.
summary: Around 1177 BCE Ramesses III beat off the Sea Peoples, a mix of raiders whose identity is still debated. Egypt won, but came out of the Late Bronze Age collapse much diminished.

cards.headline: Around 1177 BCE, raiders hit Egypt by land and by sea. Egypt won.
cards.body: So why do historians file that victory under the start of Egypt’s decline? And who were the raiders, anyway? Both answers are messier than the battle.

cards.headline: Ramesses III’s big win
cards.body: Historian Eric Cline dates it to 1177 BCE, the eighth year of Pharaoh Ramesses III’s reign. Warriors reached Egypt’s edge, some marching overland, others in ships. Ramesses beat them in battles on land and at sea, probably in or near the Nile Delta. Then he did what pharaohs did best: he advertised. The walls of his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu, near Thebes, show the fighting and rows of captives. Egypt’s side of the story, carved in stone.

cards.headline: Who were they?
cards.body: Egyptian texts name the groups one by one. The Peleset are generally believed to be the Philistines; the Sherden were probably from Sardinia. The carvings show feathered headdresses next to horned helmets, which suggests many peoples from many places, not one nation. Beyond that, their exact origins are uncertain. “Sea Peoples” is less a name than a label on a mystery box.
cards.callout: Many peoples, many places, one label

mascot.line: The most visible villain in a story isn’t always the whole explanation.

cards.headline: Winning the battle, losing the era
cards.body: Scholars once blamed the Sea Peoples for wrecking the great powers of the day, such as the Hittite empire. Recent research sees the Late Bronze Age collapse as having many causes, climate change among them, and the raiders’ role is debated. Egypt was the only major power to fight them off. Yet afterward, New Kingdom Egypt was much diminished. It survived the storm, but the whole neighborhood had changed.

title: Priests and Kings
objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt split between priests and kings.
summary: After the New Kingdom, the high priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes while kings ruled the north from Tanis. The priests also rescued robbed royal mummies.

cards.headline: After about 1069 BCE, kings ruled Egypt’s north and priests ran the south.
cards.body: The New Kingdom was over. Egypt didn’t fall; it split. And the most powerful man in the south wore a priest’s robes.

cards.headline: A priest takes the title
cards.body: Herihor was high priest of the god Amun at Karnak, in Thebes. Late in the 20th dynasty, as Egypt became disunited, he took the full title of a pharaoh and founded a line of priest-kings who ruled the south. Picture your local archbishop quietly adding “King” to his business card.

cards.headline: Two capitals
cards.body: In the 21st Dynasty the split settled in. Kings ruled Lower Egypt from Tanis, in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun at Thebes grew more and more powerful. Remember Level 1’s valleys between the peaks? This is the third: the Third Intermediate Period, when the land was divided again. Later a Libyan leader, Shoshenq, founded a new dynasty at Tanis. The one who finally took all of Egypt would come from Kush, in the south.
cards.callout: North: kings at Tanis. South: priests at Thebes.

cards.headline: Rescuing the dead kings
cards.body: Meanwhile, the royal tombs at Thebes were being robbed. Priests and officials of the 21st Dynasty gathered damaged royal mummies, rewrapped them and hid several New Kingdom kings together in a secret cache at Deir el-Bahari. It worked: nobody found it until 1881. Among the kings inside was Ramesses II. Ramesses the Great, sharing a hiding place, saved by priests.

title: The Nubian Pharaohs
objective: After this level you can describe the kings of Kush who ruled Egypt.
summary: Kush, a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, conquered Egypt in the 8th century BCE and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty. Driven out by Assyria, Kush lasted another thousand years.

cards.headline: In the 700s BCE, a kingdom from the south conquered Egypt.
cards.body: Many people have never heard of it. But Kush was no small neighbor. It was one of Africa’s earliest civilizations, and for nearly a century its kings ruled Egypt as pharaohs.

cards.headline: The kingdom up the river
cards.body: Kush was the southern part of Nubia, a region stretching south from near the Nile’s first cataract, in what is now Sudan. Remember Level 5’s rapids at Aswan, Egypt’s southern border? Kush lay beyond them, upstream. Its kings ruled from Napata, near Mount Barkal, and the cult of Egypt’s god Amun was strongly rooted there. Egypt’s new pharaohs would already know its gods.

cards.headline: Piye marches north
cards.body: In the 8th century BCE, King Piye marched into Egypt, ended its petty kingdoms and took Memphis. By about 715 BCE, under Piye and then Shabaka, all of Egypt was ruled from Kush. How do we know Piye’s side? He recorded his conquest on a great stone stela, found back home at Mount Barkal. The Kushite kings ruled as Egypt’s 25th Dynasty. The pharaohs now came from the south.

mascot.line: More pyramids than Egypt. Kush deserves a much bigger spot in the story.

cards.fact: Sudan has some 255 ancient pyramids, more than twice as many as Egypt built.
cards.context: Kushite kings were buried in pyramids. Their rule in Egypt ended after the Assyrians invaded in 671 BCE; by 654 BCE the Kushites were back in Nubia. But Kush didn’t fade. It lasted about another thousand years, later ruling from Meroe, until the king of Aksum destroyed Meroe in 350 CE. Losing Egypt was one chapter in Kush’s story, not the end.

title: Persian Rule
objective: After this level you can explain how Persia conquered Egypt.
summary: Persia’s Cambyses II conquered Egypt in 525 BCE and was crowned pharaoh. Egypt won back its independence in 404 BCE, but Persia returned in 343 BCE.

cards.headline: In 525 BCE, a Persian king put on the crown of the pharaohs.
cards.body: Kush had taken Egypt from the south. Now the Persian king Cambyses II took it, and he didn’t just seize the land. He took the job title too.

cards.headline: Crowned by the conqueror
cards.body: Cambyses II won the Battle of Pelusium in the Nile Delta, took Memphis, and Egyptian resistance collapsed. Then he had himself crowned as pharaoh. A later Persian king, Darius I, restored the priests’ privileges, had Egyptian law written down and completed or repaired a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. Foreign rulers, wearing Egyptian titles.

mascot.line: When the writer is famous and the story is juicy, check it twice.

cards.headline: Don’t believe every travel writer
cards.body: Remember Herodotus from Level 2? His 5th-century BCE visit came while Egypt was Persian. He accused Cambyses of atrocities in Egypt and put them down to madness. But Egyptian sources from Cambyses’ own time suggest those accusations must largely be discounted. A famous writer with a great story still needs checking against the evidence.

cards.headline: The last native pharaoh
cards.body: Egypt rebelled near the end of Darius’s reign, and in 404 BCE it won its independence under Amyrtaeus of Sais. Egyptian kings ruled again, but not for long. The last of them, Nectanebo II, reigned from 360 until 343 BCE, when Persia reconquered Egypt. He fled south, and after that nothing more is known of him. The line of native pharaohs didn’t end with a funeral. It simply went quiet.

title: Alexander in Egypt

cards.headline: In 332 BCE, Egypt welcomed a foreign conqueror as its deliverer.
cards.body: Alexander the Great took Egypt without a real fight. Then he set about becoming a proper pharaoh.

cards.headline: No battle needed
cards.body: Egypt was still under Persian rule when Alexander, king of Macedonia, arrived in November 332 BCE. The Persian governor, the satrap Mazaces, surrendered, and the people welcomed Alexander as their deliverer. Picture tenants throwing a party for the new landlord. After Persia, the bar was low.

cards.headline: Playing pharaoh
cards.body: At Memphis, Alexander sacrificed to the sacred Apis bull and was crowned with the double crown of the pharaohs. Remember it from Level 6? White and red together: Upper and Lower Egypt under one king. Then he went to the oracle of Amun in the Siwa oasis, where the priest greeted him as “son of Amun,” the traditional greeting for a pharaoh. A Macedonian, hailed in the pharaohs’ own words.
cards.callout: Crowned at Memphis, greeted as son of Amun at Siwa

cards.headline: A city, and a body
cards.body: Alexander founded a new city near the Nile’s western arm, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, sheltered by the island of Pharos: Alexandria. He didn’t stay to see it grow. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his general Ptolemy diverted his body to Egypt. It ended up in a golden coffin in Alexandria. Alive, Alexander left Egypt behind. Dead, he came back to stay.

title: Alexandria
objective: After this level you can describe Alexandria’s lighthouse and library.
summary: Alexandria’s Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders, and its library tried to collect every book in the world. The library faded slowly over centuries, not in one fire.

cards.headline: One city had antiquity’s most famous lighthouse and its most famous library.
cards.body: One burned a fire every night. The other, whatever you’ve heard, didn’t vanish in one great blaze.

cards.headline: A tower with a fire on top
cards.body: On the island of Pharos stood a lighthouse finished in about 280 BCE, one of the Seven Wonders of the World. It rose more than 110 metres; only the pyramids of Giza would have been taller. A spiral ramp led to the top, where a fire burned at night. It stood until an earthquake in the 1300s, and in 1477 a sultan, Qaitbay, built a fort from its ruins. Ancient recycling, on a grand scale.

cards.headline: All the books in the world
cards.body: Around 295 BCE, Ptolemy I had Demetrius of Phaleron found a library and the Mouseion, a research institute for scholars. The goal: all the books in the world. Ships entering Alexandria’s harbor were searched, and books found aboard were confiscated or copied for the collection. Imagine landing at an airport and having your paperback copied at customs.

mascot.line: Big fires make great stories. Slow neglect makes real history.

cards.headline: A slow goodbye, not one fire
cards.body: The popular story is one great fire. The evidence is messier. In 48 BCE, during Julius Caesar’s civil war, at least part of the library was damaged, yet scholars seem to have kept working there. Historians describe a slow decline through neglect and several blows over centuries, and they still debate the causes. A later tale blaming the Arab conquerors is, modern historians say, a myth. No single villain, no single night.

summary: Ptolemy, Alexander’s Macedonian general, founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt for almost 300 years. They appeared as pharaohs on temple walls while keeping their own Greek ways.

cards.headline: For almost 300 years, Egypt’s kings were Macedonian Greeks named Ptolemy.
cards.body: How does a foreign family hold a country that long? By being two kinds of ruler at once.

cards.headline: Ptolemy takes charge
cards.body: When Alexander died in 323 BCE, his Macedonian general Ptolemy became governor of Egypt, and in 305 BCE he proclaimed himself king. His dynasty ruled until 30 BCE. Naming the heirs was easy: the kings ran from Ptolemy I to Ptolemy XV. If you’ve ever lost track of which one is which, you’re in good company.

cards.headline: Two faces of one crown
cards.body: To their Egyptian subjects, the Ptolemies looked like proper pharaohs: they backed Egyptian temples and appeared on temple walls in the traditional pharaonic style. Ptolemy I also promoted Serapis, a god with Egyptian roots and Greek features, whose cult blended both religions. Remember Manetho from Level 9? He wrote his history of Egypt in Greek around 300 BCE, early in Ptolemaic rule.
cards.callout: Pharaohs on the temple walls, Greeks at home

cards.headline: Only one learned Egyptian
cards.body: Behind the temple images, the family kept its own ways. Ptolemy II married his full sister, Arsinoe II, and brother-sister marriage became a feature of the dynasty. And according to the ancient writer Plutarch, of all the Ptolemies only Cleopatra VII took the trouble to learn Egyptian. Nearly three centuries on the throne, and one ruler who could chat with Egyptians in their own language.

title: Rome's Breadbasket
objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt became the grain supply of Rome.
summary: From 30 BCE Egypt was the Roman emperor’s own province, closed to senators without permission. Its Nile-fed grain fed Rome for about four months a year.

cards.headline: For four months of every year, one ancient writer said, Rome ate Egyptian grain.
cards.body: No wonder the emperors kept Egypt on a very short leash.

cards.headline: The emperor’s own province
cards.body: In 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province, but not an ordinary one. Octavian, the future emperor Augustus, treated it as his own private kingdom, as heir to the Ptolemies. A prefect he appointed ran it, and Roman senators were forbidden to visit without the emperor’s permission. Egypt wasn’t just conquered. It was fenced off.

cards.headline: Four months of bread
cards.body: Why the fuss? Grain. Egypt’s granaries now belonged to Rome, and Egypt became the empire’s breadbasket. The historian Josephus, writing in the 1st century CE, said Egypt sent Rome enough grain to feed it for four months of the year, on top of its tax money. Four months out of twelve: a third of the city’s year, from one province.
cards.callout: Egypt fed Rome a third of the year

mascot.line: Same river, same silt. Only the address on the grain sacks changed.

title: The End of the Old Gods
objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity and later Islam replaced the old religion.
summary: Christianity spread through Egypt, and the temples closed, the Serapeum in 391 CE and Philae under Justinian. After the Arab conquest of 640 to 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim gradually.

cards.headline: Egypt’s gods outlasted every conqueror. They didn’t outlast a change of faith.
cards.body: The old religion didn’t fall in one battle. It went quiet temple by temple, from the Serapeum in 391 CE to Philae in the 6th century.

cards.headline: A new faith
cards.body: Christianity, tradition says, was brought to Alexandria by St. Mark in the first half of the 1st century CE, and it spread quickly through Egypt. Egypt’s Christians came to be called Copts, and they spoke Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language. The old tongue lived on. It just had new prayers to say.

cards.headline: The temples close
cards.body: In 391 CE the patriarch of Alexandria and his followers destroyed the city’s Serapeum, the great temple of Serapis, with Emperor Theodosius I’s encouragement, and other temples fell too. One famous holdout was Isis’s temple on the island of Philae, where the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE. It wasn’t closed until Emperor Justinian’s reign, in the 6th century, and was then made into a church.
cards.callout: Serapeum destroyed 391 CE; Philae closed in the 6th century

cards.headline: Then, slowly, Islam
cards.body: Between 640 and 642 CE, Arab forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ beat the Byzantine armies and entered Alexandria. Even then, change was slow. Egypt was mostly Christian at the conquest and became Muslim gradually over centuries; historians can’t pin down when Muslims became the majority. By the 12th century the Coptic church itself had adopted Arabic alongside Coptic. Faiths and languages rarely switch overnight.

title: Forgetting Hieroglyphs
objective: After this level you can explain how knowledge of hieroglyphs was lost.
summary: The last known hieroglyphs were carved at Philae in 394 CE. Egyptians switched to a Greek-based alphabet, and later scholars like Horapollo misread the signs as symbols.

cards.headline: For more than 1,400 years, nobody on Earth could read a hieroglyph.
cards.body: The signs never went anywhere. They stayed carved on temple walls and tombs the whole time. What vanished was anyone who knew what they said. So how does a whole civilization’s writing get forgotten?

cards.headline: The last hieroglyph
cards.body: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE, at the Temple of Isis at Philae. That’s more than four centuries after Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE (remember the end of Level 1’s timeline?). The old script had outlived the pharaohs by a long way. Its final signs are roughly cut but still clear enough to read. There was just no one left to read them.

mascot.line: Same language, new letters. Hold on to Coptic: it comes back to help later in this chapter.

cards.headline: A new alphabet
cards.body: Why stop? As Christianity spread in Egypt, people dropped hieroglyphs for an adapted form of the Greek alphabet. The language itself lived on as Coptic, the final stage of Egyptian, written in Greek letters plus seven letters borrowed from demotic. So Egyptians kept speaking their ancestors’ language while the old signs fell silent. It’s like keeping your family’s recipes but losing the handwriting they were written in.

cards.headline: Reading riddles
cards.body: Without readers, people guessed. In the 5th century CE, a Greco-Egyptian scholar named Horapollo wrote the Hieroglyphica, explaining each sign as a symbol or an allegory. He couldn’t actually read hieroglyphs himself. Renaissance scholars loved his book anyway, and the idea stuck: hieroglyphs were picture riddles, not sounds. That one wrong idea kept the door locked until the 1820s.

title: The Rosetta Stone
objective: After this level you can explain how the Rosetta Stone was found and why it mattered.
summary: French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799. It carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

cards.headline: In 1799, soldiers digging a fort’s foundations hit the key to a lost script.
cards.body: They were French troops of Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt, working near the port of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta. The broken slab they dug up was covered in writing, in three different scripts. That was the whole point.

cards.headline: One message, three scripts
cards.body: The stone carries the same decree three times. First in hieroglyphs. Then in demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting. Then in ancient Greek, the language of Egypt’s Macedonian Greek rulers. Nobody could read the first two, but scholars could still read Greek. So here was a lost script with a translation stapled on. Picture a menu printed in a language you can’t read, right beside one you can.
cards.callout: Hieroglyphs + demotic + Greek = one message

mascot.line: The key to a whole lost script is, word for word, a bit of priestly paperwork.

cards.headline: What it actually says
cards.body: Don’t expect a treasure map. The decree was issued in 196 BCE by priests of a temple in Memphis, confirming the Macedonian king Ptolemy V as a divine ruler. It’s official temple business. The words were never the exciting part. The exciting part was hearing the same thing said three ways.

cards.headline: From Rashid to London
cards.body: The French didn’t keep their find. After the French surrender in Egypt in 1801, the stone passed to the British. It has been on display in the British Museum since 1802, leaving only once, when it was moved to safety during the First World War. Whether it should stay there is a live argument, and it gets its own level later in this chapter.

title: Champollion Cracks the Code
objective: After this level you can explain how Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs.
summary: Thomas Young read the sounds of Ptolemy’s name; in 1822 Champollion showed that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with signs for ideas.

cards.headline: In 1822, a scholar burst in on his brother, cried “I’ve got it!” and fainted.
cards.body: In French, he said “Je tiens mon affaire!” The scholar was Jean-François Champollion, and what he’d got was the key to hieroglyphs. But he wasn’t the first to get a foot in the door. An English scientist had already shown that some signs spelled the sounds of a name.

cards.headline: Thomas Young’s head start
cards.body: Thomas Young was an English physicist, also famous for his work on light, who began studying the Rosetta Stone in 1814. He showed that some hieroglyphs on the stone spelled out the sounds of a royal name: Ptolemy. He also made major advances in reading demotic. That was a real crack in the wall. Most of the wall was still standing.

mascot.line: Sometimes the breakthrough isn’t a flash of genius. It’s just counting carefully.

cards.headline: Too many signs
cards.body: Champollion tried counting. The hieroglyphic text on the Rosetta Stone uses 1,419 signs, while the Greek version has only 486 words. If every sign were a whole idea, those numbers should be much closer. So many signs had to stand for sounds, mixed with others that stood for whole ideas or objects. Hieroglyphs weren’t picture riddles after all. They were writing down a spoken language.
cards.callout: 1,419 signs for 486 words: too many for pictures alone

cards.headline: Not just foreign names
cards.body: Maybe sound signs were only a trick for foreign names like Ptolemy? Champollion knew Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which helped him hear the sounds behind the signs. With it he read the name of Ramesses, a native Egyptian king. Egyptians had been writing sounds all along. On 27 September 1822 he announced it in Paris, with Thomas Young in the audience. The door locked since 394 CE was open.

title: Egyptomania
objective: After this level you can explain the craze for all things Egyptian in Europe.
summary: Napoleon’s scholars and their Description de l’Égypte, then Champollion’s decipherment, set off Egyptomania: Egyptian-style buildings and real obelisks shipped to London and New York.

cards.headline: Napoleon invaded Egypt with an army and about 150 artists and scientists.
cards.body: The army’s campaign ended in surrender. The scholars did better: they helped set off a craze for ancient Egypt that swept Europe and America.

cards.headline: A country in picture books
cards.body: The 1798 invasion doubled as the first large-scale scientific expedition to Egypt. The scholars measured and drew everything they could. Back in France, their record became the Description de l’Égypte, published from 1809 with huge prints of pyramids, temples and other antiquities. For readers at home, it was like having Egypt delivered to the library in giant installments.

mascot.line: Next time you see an Egyptian-style gate or column far from Egypt, you’ve spotted a bit of Egyptomania.

cards.headline: Egyptomania
cards.body: Then came Champollion’s decipherment in 1822 (Level 93), and interest surged again. The craze got a name: Egyptomania. Architects mined the Description for Egyptian designs. In the United States the first wave was mostly buildings, including cemetery architecture and the Washington Monument, begun in 1848. Some of that craze is still standing in Washington.

cards.headline: Cleopatra’s Needles
cards.body: Some people wanted the real thing. Two granite obelisks, carved about 3,500 years ago for Thutmose III, were given away by Egypt’s government: one was raised in London in 1878, the other in New York’s Central Park in 1881. They’re called Cleopatra’s Needles because the Romans moved them to Alexandria, to a temple conceived by Cleopatra. They were already more than a thousand years old in her day.

title: Finding Tutankhamun
objective: After this level you can explain Howard Carter's discovery in 1922.
summary: Funded by Lord Carnarvon, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun’s largely intact tomb in November 1922 and spent about ten years recording its 5,398 objects.

cards.headline: By 1922, the man paying for the dig was ready to give up.
cards.body: Lord Carnarvon had funded Howard Carter’s digging for years with little to show for it. Carter talked him into one final season. It began on 1 November 1922, and three days later, a step appeared.

cards.headline: A step under a hut
cards.body: On 4 November, Carter’s team found a step cut into the bedrock beneath the remains of ancient workmen’s huts, about four metres below the entrance of Ramesses VI’s tomb. Soon they had exposed a sealed doorway. Carter covered it back up and cabled Carnarvon in England: “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley.” The tomb had spent centuries under a building site.

mascot.line: Even the most famous line in archaeology got a second draft.

cards.headline: Wonderful things
cards.body: On 26 November, with Carnarvon beside him, Carter made a small hole in a second sealed doorway, stamped with Tutankhamun’s seals, and held up a candle. Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. That night Carter’s journal recorded his reply: “Yes, it is wonderful.” His later popular account polished it into the line everyone quotes: “Yes, wonderful things.”

cards.headline: Ten years of homework
cards.body: The tomb was largely intact, the first known intact royal burial from ancient Egypt. Carter’s team numbered its 5,398 objects and spent about ten years clearing and recording them. Their notes, photographs and drawings are kept at the Griffith Institute in Oxford. The gold made the headlines. The paperwork made it science.

title: Studying Egypt Today
objective: After this level you can describe modern tools like scans and satellite images.
summary: Muon detectors find hidden spaces in the Great Pyramid, CT scans unwrap mummies digitally, and infrared satellite images reveal buried mud-brick buildings.

cards.headline: Archaeologists can now look inside a pyramid without moving a single block.
cards.body: They can unwrap a pharaoh without touching a thread, and spot buried buildings from orbit. Egypt is still giving up secrets. What’s changed is the tools.

cards.headline: An X-ray lit by the sky
cards.body: Muons are particles made when cosmic rays hit our atmosphere, and they rain down constantly. Stone absorbs some of them, so detectors can map empty spaces inside a pyramid. In 2017 the ScanPyramids team reported a big void at least 30 metres long above the Great Pyramid’s Grand Gallery. In 2023, muons located a corridor about 9 metres long behind the north face, and a camera pushed inside confirmed it.

mascot.line: No scissors, no unrolling: just a scanner and a lot of patience.

cards.headline: Unwrapping without unwrapping
cards.body: Amenhotep I’s mummy was so finely wrapped, with flower garlands and a lifelike mask, that no one opened it in modern times. In 2021, radiologist Sahar Saleem and Egyptologist Zahi Hawass unwrapped it digitally with CT scans. Inside was a man about 35 years old, with good teeth and 30 amulets tucked into his wrappings. The mask stayed on. The secrets came out.

cards.headline: Archaeology from orbit
cards.body: Sarah Parcak of the University of Alabama at Birmingham processes satellite images to see in infrared, which your eyes can’t. In the desert, it picks up moisture differences in the ground above buried mud bricks, tracing the outlines of vanished buildings. Her team mapped the street grid of Tanis, once a capital in the Nile Delta, and tracked tomb looting after 2011. Some of the best new digging starts with no digging at all.
