title: Who Owns the Past?
objective: After this level you can explain debates over returning ancient objects to Egypt.
summary: Zahi Hawass wants the Rosetta Stone and Nefertiti bust returned; the museums in London and Berlin defend how they got them. Egypt opened the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2025.

cards.headline: The Rosetta Stone has sat in London since 1802. Many want it back.
cards.body: Who should keep objects taken from Egypt long ago? It’s a real argument, and both sides have reasons. Here are both cases, who makes them, and one very large new building.

cards.headline: The case for return
cards.body: In 2022, Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, launched a petition for the Rosetta Stone’s return that passed 100,000 signatures. He also wants the bust of Nefertiti back from Berlin and the Dendera Zodiac from the Louvre, saying these unique objects belong in Egypt. On Nefertiti he goes further: he argues the bust, found in 1912 and taken to Berlin in 1913, left Egypt illegally.

mascot.line: When two sides tell the same story differently, it helps to know exactly who is saying what.

cards.headline: The museums’ case
cards.body: The British Museum says the Rosetta Stone came to Britain under an 1801 treaty signed by a representative of Egypt. It adds that Egypt’s government has made no formal request, and that most known copies of the decree are already in Egypt. Berlin’s museum points out that the Nefertiti bust left through an official division of finds in 1913, overseen by an inspector of Egypt’s antiquities service. Same objects, very different stories.

cards.headline: A new home by the pyramids
cards.body: Egypt has also made its point in concrete. The Grand Egyptian Museum, near the Great Pyramid at Giza, officially opened on 1 November 2025 with about 100,000 artifacts. For the first time since its discovery, Tutankhamun’s entire collection is shown together. Remember Carter’s 5,398 numbered objects from Level 95? They’re finally all in one place.

title: Myths About Egypt
objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like aliens building the pyramids.
summary: Paid workers, not slaves, built the Giza pyramids; Merer’s logbook shows human crews at work; the curse and Cleopatra’s looks rest on thin evidence.

cards.headline: Ancient Egypt collects myths the way a pyramid collects sand.
cards.body: Take the famous curse on Tutankhamun’s tomb: Howard Carter, the man who opened it in 1922, lived until 1939. Some myths started with ancient writers, and some with Hollywood. The fix is always the same: check the evidence.

cards.headline: Myth: slaves built the pyramids
cards.body: The picture of whipped slaves comes from Herodotus (yes, Level 2’s “gift of the river” man), misreadings of the Bible’s book of Exodus, and Hollywood films. The ground tells another story. Near the Giza pyramids, archaeologists found workers’ districts with bakeries and workshops, and workers’ tombs close to the pyramids, some naming the dead. Most archaeologists now think paid laborers built them.

mascot.line: The best answer to a wild theory is often a very boring document.

cards.headline: Myth: aliens did it
cards.body: The builders left paperwork. In 2013, archaeologists at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea found the oldest known inscribed papyri, including the logbook of an official named Merer. His crew shipped limestone by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza for Khufu’s pyramid, and he logged the work in half-day entries. Aliens, as far as anyone knows, don’t fill in timesheets.

cards.headline: Myth: we know Cleopatra’s face
cards.body: People argue hotly about Cleopatra’s looks, but the evidence is thin. She belonged to a Macedonian Greek dynasty, yet even her mother’s identity is uncertain, and her coins and portrait busts don’t all agree. Plutarch, writing long after, said her beauty was “not altogether incomparable,” but that talking with her had “an irresistible charm.” Egypt’s most famous face is one of its least certain.

cards.headline: You use ancient Egypt daily: in your calendar, your alphabet and your paper.
cards.body: Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE, but pieces of it never left. Here are three hiding in plain sight.

cards.headline: Your calendar
cards.body: In 46 BCE, Julius Caesar reformed Rome’s calendar by adopting the Egyptian solar calendar, advised by Sosigenes, an astronomer from Alexandria. The year became 365 and a quarter days, with an extra day every fourth year. Pope Gregory XIII fine-tuned it in 1582, and his Gregorian calendar gradually replaced Caesar’s. Every leap day has an Egyptian ancestor.

mascot.line: A for ox. Once you see the horns, you can’t unsee them.

cards.headline: Your alphabet
cards.body: Look at the letter A. The inventors of the alphabet were influenced by Egyptian writing, and A goes back to a sign shaped like an ox’s head. Early Semitic writing in Sinai adopted it around 1500 BCE. The Phoenicians called it aleph, meaning “ox,” and the Greeks renamed it alpha and used it for a vowel. Turn a capital A upside down and imagine the horns.

cards.headline: Your paper
cards.body: The word “paper” comes from papyrus, the Egyptian writing material. The Greeks adopted papyrus, and the Roman Empire used it widely. Books and documents on papyrus were still being made, now and then, until about the 12th century. So whenever you ask for a sheet of paper, you’re naming an Egyptian invention.
